articles.title: Steam Machines have returned: all the news about Valve’s new hardware universe
articles.summary: Valve never stopped quietly working on Steam Machines. Now, they are back, and we’re following the news here.
articles.body: In 2012, The Verge broke the news that Valve was making a game console. Gabe Newell himself dished on the company’s grand plans. By 2015, the “Steam Machines” had utterly flopped. But Valve never stopped quietly working on the idea. The Steam Deck handheld became the seed for a grand reboot of Valve’s console and headset ambitions. And now, Steam Machines are back. The new Steam Machine is for your TV, the Steam Controller is for your hands, and the Steam Frame is for your face — and they might just be the start. The company hinted there might be more SteamOS hardware later on. [Media: We’re tracking Valve’s rebooted hardware plans in this Verge StoryStream. And if you want to know how we got here, it also contains our original Steam Machine coverage — going back over a decade.

articles.title: Valve describes just how brutal RAM negotiations are in 2026
articles.summary: Valve’s Steam Machine is expensive, but in an interview with Gamers Nexus, Valve employees spell out how getting memory for the living room PC isn’t easy.
articles.body: Valve’s Steam Machine finally has a price: a whopping $1,049 for the 512GB configuration or $1,349 for the 2TB version. And those are without bundled controllers, which drive up the cost more. The prices are so high in part because Valve isn’t subsidizing the hardware, and the company has already indicated that the component crisis forced it to reconsider its initial pricing plans. In an interview with the YouTube channel Gamers Nexus, Valve engineers discussed the reality of sourcing RAM in 2026, with take-it-or-leave-it prices as memory and other components remain in short supply, from only a few vendors like Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix. Here’s the relevant portion, starting at 12:48 in Gamers Nexus’s Steam Machine review: > Gamers Nexus: Were you able to lock in contracts for memory with the suppliers directly or did you have to jump through a bunch of hoops? > Valve’s Pierre-Loup Griffais: Look, there’s no contracts. There’s nothing. Those guys… they give us a price every month or something and they say, ‘you can buy that many,’ and it’s yes or no. And if we say no, then they never talk to us again. [Media: Valve, of course, isn’t the only company in a bind over memory shortages, as the crunch is forcing many hardware makers to make significant pricing changes. Even Apple CEO Tim Cook is warning of incoming price hikes for iPhones, Macs, and other devices. And the RAM crunch isn’t projected to get better anytime soon. Valve originally told Gamers Nexus that it would be shipping Steam Machines with either one stick of 16GB of RAM or two sticks of 8GB of RAM, with the number of stick inside depending “on the supply that we can secure,” Griffais says. According to Gamers Nexus, “dual channel will objectively perform better than single channel,” but Valve’s Yazan Aldehayyat says that in the company’s tests, having one stick or two doesn’t make “any measurable difference” while playing games. However, after Gamers Nexus’s initial review was published, Valve said to the channel that all Steam Machine units will come with 1 stick of 16GB of RAM, though noted that “it’s possible that this might change in future builds.” Valve hasn’t shared its original planned price for the Steam Machine. But the recent price increases to the Steam Deck OLED — up $240 for the 512GB version, and up $300 for the 1TB version — “should give you a ballpark estimate of how much the Steam Machine’s target had moved,” according to an Aftermath interview with Valve. Subtracting those same price hikes from the current Steam Machine prices nets out at theoretical original prices of $809 for the 512GB model and $1,049 for the 2TB model. Those prices are still high, but not as tough to swallow as what Valve officially revealed today. Update, June 24th: Valve now says all Steam Machines will come with one stick of 16GB of RAM.

articles.title: Fortnite Kingdom Hearts Collaboration, Including Sora Skin, Lands This Week
articles.summary: Fortnite has officially confirmed its long-awaited Kingdom Hearts collaboration, with teases for at least four skins.
articles.body:
Fortnite has officially confirmed its long-awaited Kingdom Hearts collaboration, with teases for at least four skins.

A brief teaser trailer posted to Fortnite's social channels shows Kingdom Hearts poster boy Sora picking up the series' iconic keyblade and posing for the camera. Yep, there's no doubt here — Sora is definitely becoming a Fortnite skin.

Text-based teasers also released by developer Epic Games suggest three other Kingdom Hearts characters are also coming along for the ride, including Riku, Kairi and Roxas. (Sadly, there's no sign of Mickey yet — though the idea of him cranking 90's while holding a shotgun seems unlikely.)

SORA TEASER TRAILER WITH SOUND pic.twitter.com/5MeCW3WxEA — Shiina (@ShiinaBR) September 13, 2026

SORA TEASER TRAILER WITH SOUND pic.twitter.com/5MeCW3WxEA

Kingdom Hearts will be the latest gaming franchise to join Fortnite during Override, its current video game-themed season, which has already added Sonic the Hedgehog, Shadow the Hedgehog, Dr. Robotnik, Crash Bandicoot and Mega Man, among others. Other upcoming additions have also been rumoured, with fans crossing their fingers for representation from Persona and Final Fantasy 7.

Override is currently having something of a cooler reception among fans than Runners, Fortnite's previous last season which went down as one of the game's best. The playerbase seems split over whether Fortnite's Pokémon-like Sprites need to be retired or revamped to still feel fresh, and player numbers have dipped slightly from this summer's recent highs.

As ever, Fortnite is already gearing itself up for its annual end-of-year festivities, with the Halloween-themed Fortnitemares set to arrive next month. One work-in-progress building on the current battle royale Island looks suspiciously like a Five Nights at Freddy's reference, which may well be a tie-in for that. And then there are already whispers that the game will transition into another month-long mini-season in November, with One Piece now being tipped as part of the fun.

Kingdom Hearts 4 , meanwhile, is in development at Square Enix for PC and consoles and is due out next year.

articles.title: Almeida abre la puerta a unos Juegos Olímpicos en Madrid: "Un reto que nos vamos a plantear"
articles.standfirst: La siguiente opción que tendría la capital de España para presentar una candidatura es de cara a 2036
articles.summary: La siguiente opción que tendría la capital de España para presentar una candidatura es de cara a 2036
articles.body: El alcalde de Madrid, José Luis Martínez Almeida, aseguró este lunes que es al Comité Olímpico Internacional (COI) al que le "interesa" que Madrid acoja unos Juegos Olímpicos: "Es un reto que nos vamos a plantear, y vamos a tener que tomar decisiones". En un desayuno organizado por el Club Siglo XXI, el alcalde de Madrid, a preguntas de los periodistas, aseveró que al Comité Olímpico Internacional le "conviene" que Madrid sea sede de unos Juegos Olímpicos, porque la capital española es una ciudad con una "capacidad" transformadora. Por eso, "no desde la certeza, pero sí desde la confianza", expresó que Madrid será una ciudad "designada": "Estoy seguro de que Madrid es una sede natural para los Juegos Olímpicos", agregó. "Lo que no nos podemos permitir -añadió- es que nos pase lo que nos pasó en las tres candidaturas anteriores (...) éramos la mejor candidatura por diferencia y caímos en la primera votación por Estambul y eso no nos puede volver a pasar", resumió. Madrid, que ya se postuló, sin éxito, a albergar los Juegos Olímpicos de 2012, 2016 y 2020, tendría que concurrir con una candidatura a los Juegos de 2036, puesto que los de 2028 se celebrarán en Los Ángeles (Estados Unidos) y los de 2032 en Brisbane (Australia).

articles.title: Zack Snyder’s The Last Photograph Is an Attempt at a Violent Arthouse Indie About His Own Need to Capture Images
articles.summary: Zack Snyder’s attempt at a violent arthouse indie (about his own need to capture images) ends up on emotionless autopilot.
articles.body:
This review is based on a screening timed to the Toronto International Film Festival. The Last Photograph does not currently have a release date.

A trudging revenge saga that points to self-critique, Zack Snyder’s long-gestating passion project The Last Photograph is filled with big ideas that go nowhere. Premiering at the Toronto International Film Festival in the hopes of finding a distributor, the film’s lone screening was preceded by an appearance from Snyder where he joked that TIFF’s audience might be the only ones to ever see it. Afterward, it felt more like a premonition, given the movie’s languorous 135 minutes of indistinguishable landscapes and unvarnished cinematic ugliness, which result in a film that feels much longer in practice.

Beginning at a child’s fancy, exclusive birthday party in Colombia, an American diplomat is shot dead, while his son and daughter are abducted by ruthless goons, who kill all the guests point blank — kids included. There’s an unflinching quality to Snyder’s depiction of violence here, but by opening The Last Photograph this way, it induces a numbing effect, wherein the bloodshed loses its luster after being repeated ad nauseam, with little variation. In an adjacent room, hired party photographer Joe Wallace (Fra Fee), an American in hiding, has sex with a waitress as the shots ring out, prompting him to zip up his pants and grab his camera just in time to see the diplomat’s wife, Catherine (Costanza Andrade), executed with malice. As she lays dying, he trains his lens on her and asks for forgiveness instead of offering help.

The big idea here is Joe’s calling to capture the world’s violence through his camera, though it’s not one that Snyder meaningfully explores, despite it frequently coming up. Joe isn’t even really the film’s main character; that would be the diplomat’s vengeful brother Ethan (Stuart Martin), a former special operative who was once involved with Catherine, and carries a topless polaroid of her in his pocket. It’s one of numerous instances of concocted, contrived female nudity; as much as Snyder might aim for tastefulness, he often veers towards titillation, a distinction emblematic of his “everything, all at once” heightened visual approach.

Working as a shepherd in remote mountains, Ethan learns of the deaths and kidnappings when Joe’s photograph of Catherine appears in a newspaper. So, he tracks him down in the hopes of identifying the killers and dealing with them himself, while rescuing the kidnapped children. What follows is, in theory, a perilous two-man journey across an unforgiving landscape. However, it ends up a meandering walkabout through thundering emotional emptiness, set against a bizarre, deeply racist concoction of South America populated by savage, predatory tribespeople who make for easy cannon fodder, continuing what some describe as a politically and culturally retrograde streak across Snyder’s filmography.

Joe and Ethan spend much of the movie side by side, though they barely speak to one another — except to state the movie’s themes out loud a dozen times — giving us a boring interpersonal dynamic that undergoes little metamorphosis by the end. The Last Photographs hints at the difficulty of change through its frequent shots (and tattoos, and TV broadcasts) of emerging butterflies, but like most concepts strewn across the movie, this ends up only skin deep.

An idea Snyder keeps returning to is Joe’s compulsion to shoot photos, alongside Ethan’s to shoot any target that moves, mirroring camera and muzzle flashes in moments of eruptive violence. However, both lead characters — gruff, stoic men who only express themselves in moments of severe anguish — are so closed off as to never form an actual relationship. It’s a buddy movie where the leads aren’t remotely friendly, or even really adversarial, leading to a joyless journey bereft of energy or allure.

Snyder tries, at times, to introduce questions of beauty and brutality coexisting, especially through the prism of Joe, but his alleged adrenaline junkiness is something spoken about in dialogue rather than actually expressed (the only thing we learn about him is that he’s a literal junkie; he shoots heroin in practically every scene). There’s never a moment of genuine thrill or curiosity when Joe pulls out his camera for the umpteenth time, as we never once see the world through his lens — an especially bizarre omission for a film that is, in part, an inquiry into photographic imagery.

The Last Photograph has been in development for 15 years, so it’s certainly not a knockoff of anything recent, but Alex Garland’s Civil War is a much more adept depiction of this idea. Instead of interrogating the need to capture images of violence — let alone the images themselves — Snyder instead loops back on some of the ideas he’s toyed with before, in big studio productions like Sucker Punch and Batman v. Superman . But his variations on these themes are never interesting enough to warrant an audiovisual retrospective. It’s really just more of the same, exactly as you’ve seen it before.

Martin, for his part, is appropriately gruff and imposing as Ethan, a ruthless killer with a past connection to this land, though not one that meaningfully informs his journey to rescue his nephew and niece. Granted, there’s an implied sincerity to the premise; Snyder, having dealt with the death of a child, imbues Ethan with a righteous fury that seemingly can’t be quenched, and a sense of nihilism that invades both characters’ psyches on occasion. But these moments of genuine psychodrama are few and far between. They usually make way for Ethan to dispense with his targets with extreme ease and proficiency, though the movie seldom lets these moments breathe; even as a series of righteous reprisals, there’s no fist-pumping adrenaline to the violence, or even mournful reflection. It’s just as-is; a whole lot of nothing, captured from an objective vantage.

For the most part, Snyder’s seemingly improvised cinematography (with its razor thin plane of focus) captures people, actions and events at their most functional and literal, despite the movie frequently hinting at a kind of forested fantasia through roving wide lenses that warp each space. However, nothing in the present sparks intrigue. Repetitive flashbacks are ultimately the flavor of the day, adding little to what’s already known, and weighing down the story in the process. Just when things threaten to get interesting by putting Ethan on the backfoot, he ends up with militarized support from former comrades who make his journey even easier.

Things certainly happen in The Last Photograph, in that it contains a handful of shootouts. But amid both the action and the shout-y drama, Snyder maintains little sense of place, turning each instance into an isolated snippet, rather than part of a meaningful whole. These scattered moments are interspersed with echoing stretches of nothing in particular, where the score (by Hans Zimmer, Omer Benyamin and Steven Doar) equals little more than errant rumblings, and the landscape photography adds few dimensions to what little already transpires between its stunted leads.

Joe and Ethan appear to be sides to how Snyder sees himself, as a man driven to both voyeurism and violent instincts. However, his indiscriminate use of tools like slow-motion — focused on everything from gunplay to Ethan making a sandwich — continues to plague him as a filmmaker, yielding a work of flattened feelings and images that fail to conjure the slightest emotion.

articles.title: Discover Your Next Must-Play PC Game With Steam Hype
articles.body:
Between respectably powerful, cheap laptops, handhelds like the Steam Deck and the new generation of mini-PCs like the Steam Machine, it’s easier than ever to dip into the vast ocean of PC games. But that also presents challenges and the hardest part is deciding what to play when there’s often upwards of a hundred releases every day on Steam alone. Even if you uncharitably assume that 95% is trash, that’s still five-plus notable, worthwhile games. Every. Single. Day.

Filtering out the good from the bad is a full-time job. Luckily it’s my full-time job! I’m Dominic Tarason, and I’m the staff writer on Steam Hype , a brand new website for people who love PC gaming but are bewildered by the sheer volume of new games constantly hitting Steam. I’m here to help you discover your next must-play PC game, whether it’s something that’s been slowly gaining hype over time and has just released, or a brand new indie that’s come out of nowhere. Better still, everything you’ll find on Steam Hype is hand-picked either by myself or someone else on the team – it isn’t powered by faceless algorithms or AI, but by real humans (I promise I’m real!) who have encyclopaedic knowledge of all things PC.

Although Steam Hype has only just officially launched, we’ve been working away on it in the background for the last few months. As such, there’s a bunch of interesting stuff to read already, with round-ups meant to get you up to speed with entire genres. The PC can’t be beaten by RPGs, so we’ve got a five-part crash course covering the finest Classic CRPGs , the best Action RPGs , essential JRPGs and–for the oldheads–must-have old-school Dungeon RPGs . We’ve also got an explainer on the ever-booming world of retro first-person shooters , whether you want something from the current crop or are hunting for mods for a ‘90s classic.

We’re slowly ramping up our review coverage, too, with a focus on the unusual and the semi-obscure, like PS360 throwback FPS Twisted Tower or cult hit neo-retro horror adventure Endacopia . We’re also looking back at the games that weren’t quite there at launch, but have grown into gems – a real perk of PC development. A great example is the now-excellent mech tactics game Phantom Brigade .

No PC gamer worth their salt should skip on our list of great PC exclusives either ; over a hundred (and growing) experiences you can’t get anywhere else, and a great place for console folks looking to expand their gaming horizons. And that’s just what we’ve got ready lined up for launch – Steam Hype is going to keep on growing, keep on expanding, and keep on demystifying the world of PC games.

We’re so excited to show you everything that Steam Hype has to offer, putting our decades of knowledge to make your day a little more hypeworthy. Join us and be part of the next generation .

Steam Hype is the latest site in the Hookshot network, joining Nintendo Life , Push Square , Pure Xbox and the retro-centric Time Extension to cover all corners of the gaming universe. Hookshot is also partnered with the tech experts at Digital Foundry and is partnered commercially with IGN. As Hookshot’s dedicated PC gaming site, it’s got news of the latest releases , updates and mod drops , plus weekly roundups and a must-play monthly playlist to help you keep up with the never-ending deluge of new experiences.

articles.title: Capcom Opens First U.S. Merch Store as a Pop-Up in Los Angeles
articles.summary: Capcom, publisher of not one or two but three well-received games so far this year (Resident Evil Requiem, Pragmata, and Onimusha: Way of the Sword) is opening its first retail store in the U.S. It'll be a pop-up in Little Akihabara in Little Tokyo, Los Angeles. The grand opening is this Saturday, September 19, and "a limited number" of attendees have a chance to play the upcoming Mega Man: Dual Override on Saturday and Sunday. Meanwhile, the first 50 shoppers on the 19th and 20th will receive "a limited-edition Tokyo Game Show handkerchief featuring popular Capcom games."
articles.body:
Capcom, publisher of not one or two but three well-received games so far this year (Resident Evil Requiem, Pragmata, and Onimusha: Way of the Sword), is opening its first retail store in the U.S. It'll be a pop-up in Little Akihabara in Little Tokyo, Los Angeles. The grand opening is this Saturday, September 19, and "a limited number" of attendees have a chance to play the upcoming Mega Man: Dual Override on Saturday and Sunday. Meanwhile, the first 50 shoppers on the 19th and 20th will receive "a limited-edition Tokyo Game Show handkerchief featuring popular Capcom games."

The pop-up will run through October 18 at Little Akihabara Popup Shop & Live, located at 319 E 2nd St. #122. Hours are from 12pm–7pm. Merch items include plushies, T-shirts, keychains, and more. Check some of the items out in the gallery below.

The company also teased that the store will feature life-size statues of "fan-favorite" characters from Street Fighter and Mega Man and additional playable demos of other Capcom games.

Capcom has had a great year so far, with the aforementioned Resident Evil Requiem topping 7 million units sold , Pragmata topping 2 million units sold in just over two weeks – which Capcom says makes a sequel likely , and Onimusha: Way of the Sword picked up a 10 out of 10 review score from IGN. Moving forward, Capcom wants to " re-activate IPs that haven’t had a new title launch recently, " which could mean anything from Dino Crisis to Dead Rising or Lost Planet, to name a few.

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked , and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch . He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan .

articles.title: Upcoming PS5 Games: The Future of PlayStation Exclusives
articles.summary: Checking in with the PS5 generation.
articles.body:
After what seemed like the end of console exclusives, Xbox and PlayStation are officially getting back into the game. (Let's be real, Nintendo never left it .)

While the past generation of PS5-exclusive games eventually made their way to PC, Sony announced in May 2026 that future single-player games will actually be exclusive to the console. That was a recent announcement, so things are being ironed out, and some games that have been development will still see a simultaneous launch on both systems.

Without further ado, here’s what games you have to look forward to under the PlayStation banner in 2026 and beyond.

Marvel’s Wolverine - September 15, 2026 (PS5 Exclusive)

The next PS5-exclusive game comes from none other than Insomniac, the studio behind the massive Spider-Man and Miles Morales games. While they’re moving away from your friendly neighborhood web-swinger, the studio is keeping things in the Marvel family with a new take on the clawed Canadian mutant. The linear action game will loop in other familiar faces from the world of X-Men , and Insomniac has promised plenty of gore and… other things ... that warranted an M-rating.

Phantom Blade Zero - October 29, 2026 (Timed PS5 and PC Exclusive)

This Wuxia-inspired action game comes from Chinese studio S-Game, and is technically the fifth entry in the Phantom Blade series . The original games were developed in RPGMaker and translated as ‘Rainblood,’ and while the new entry looks graphically stunning, studio founder Soulframe Liang stated in a PS blogpost that he sees Zero as a “spiritual rebirth” of those originals.

After a short delay from earlier this year, Phantom Blade Zero is set to launch on October 29, 2026 on both PS5 and PC. It’s not a full exclusive, however, and will be released on Xbox and Switch 2 a full year later , in Fall 2027.

Until Dawn 2 - January 28, 2027 (PS5 Exclusive)

An Until Dawn sequel was revealed at the same State of Play as God of War Laufey. While we don’t have too many details, our first trailer showed off a new cast of characters, including Neil Newbon of Astarion fame . The story will follow a group of fake ghost hunters looking for clicks on a ‘haunted’ island, who ultimately find themselves wrapped up in a very real and deadly crisis. Expect the return of big consequence decision making, tons of possible endings, and some gnarly cutscenes.

God of War Laufey - February 16, 2027 (PS5 Exclusive)

The next mainline God of War game was revealed at a State of Play in February 2026. God of War Laufey will feature none other than Kratos’s wife and Atreus’s mother, Faye , in a story that overlaps with the timeline of the 2019 reboot and Ragnarok.

After passing away in Midgard, Faye wakes up in the Everywhen, a plane in the afterlife with gods from across mythologies vying for power. Her journey isn’t over, and she still wants to support her family. She won’t be alone, either, getting help from a gelatinous cube and a ribbon. Yep, chew on that.

God of War Laufey is officially set to be released exclusively on PS5 on February 16, 2027. You can check out our full interview with the team at Santa Monica Studio for more.

Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet - TBA (PS5 Exclusive)

To be honest, there’s a chance Naughty Dog skips the PS5 generation entirely. The studio's last new game was technically The Last of Us: Part 2 , just before the current-gen console's launch. Thankfully, we now know what the company has been working on in the interim, and it’s in fact an entirely new IP .

Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet places you as Jordan A. Mun, a rogue bounty hunter stuck on the remote planet of Sempiria in an alternate, 80’s-inspired version of the future. Details have been sparse since the game’s announcement, but Neil Druckmann has commented on the game’s title and focus on faith .

There’s been no word on a release date, though Naughty Dog employees have reportedly been under quite the crunch to get through the end of development.

The only multiplayer game on this list is also one I wouldn’t quite get your hopes up about. Fairgame$ was announced all the way back in 2023 , though reports of the new IP date back to 2021 . The heist shooter was supposed to be the debut game from Haven Studios, but the team had also been tapped to support the ill-fated Concord. The studio's founding member, Jade Raymond , and its creative director , both left the studio in 2025, a generally massive year for studio shuffles under PlayStation.

Last we heard, Fairgame$ was delayed to 2026, which is… right now. After the success of Helldivers 2 , it seems pretty certain that if this one does launch, it'll also be playable on PC. We’ll let you know if we hear anything more.

Bonus: GTA 6 - November 19, 2026 (Timed Console Exclusive)

We're straying away from first-party PlayStation titles, but its worth calling out what's expected to be the biggest game launch of all time . While GTA 6 isn't under PlayStation and won’t be exclusive to the PS5, it will in fact be exclusive to consoles . That means you’ll only be able to play it on the PS5 or Xbox Series X/S for a yet to be announced window of time after its release.

Blythe (she/her) is an Audience Development Coordinator at IGN who spends way too much time in character customization screens and tracking down collectibles.

articles.title: Steven Spielberg's Hook: 35th Anniversary 4K Steelbook Is Up for Preorder
articles.summary: Spielberg's Hook came out 35 years ago, and to celebrate Sony is releasing a 4K steelbook edition with all-new bonus features.
articles.body:
Hook, Steven Spielberg’s 1991 movie about a grown-up Peter Pan, is officially 35 years old. To celebrate the milestone, Sony is releasing a new 4K steelbook version. It’s up for preorder now ( see it at Amazon ) for $39.99, with a release date of November 17.

It comes in a fetching case adorned with the same cover art as the 1992 VHS edition. It also has two all-new bonus features that are presented in full 4K. So far it's only up at Amazon, but I'll add more retailers as the listings go live. Read on for the details.

Hook 35th Anniversary Steelbook Edition (4K UHD + Digital)

This movie is exceptionally star-studded. It has Robin Williams as Peter Pan, of course. It has Julia Roberts as Tinkerbell, as well as Dustin Hoffman as an absolutely delightful Captain Hook. Dame Maggie Smith plays an elderly Wendy Moira Angela Darling, and Bob Hoskins absolutely kills it as Smee (he would go on play Mario in Super Mario Bros. just two years later). You can’t beat a cast like that.

I’m well aware that Hook has its detractors . But it’s clear (to this elder Millennial, anyway) that the movie’s biggest critics weren’t its target audience when it came out. I adored this movie as a kid, and I’ve shown it to my own kids, who also enjoyed it decades later.

What's so great about it? It has Robin Williams at the height of his powers, along with the rest of the cast mentioned above, including Julia Roberts right when she’s launching her mega-star career. Plus, it has a colorful food fight, a room full of clocks, and a dog barking the word “Hook.” What’s not to love?

articles.title: Lies of P Trademark Appears to Spell Out Sequel's Name
articles.summary: Lies of P looks set to be followed by Wonders of O, according to a new trademark listing.
articles.body:
Lies of P looks set to be followed by "Wonders of O," according to a new trademark listing.

Developer Neowiz appears to have trademarked the title via the EU Intellectual Property Office , for use in an upcoming game (as spotted by PhraseMaker ).

But while "P" was a reference to Pinocchio, what could "O" stand for? Well, fans of the puppet-starring Soulslike already think they know the answer, following various teases pointing to The Wizard of Oz and its character Dorothy — including a cameo from the Kansas heroine during the game's post-credits scene.

Announced as being in full development earlier this year , the follow-up to Lies of P has long been expected to center on characters from L. Frank Baum's Oz series, which is what our guess for the "O" would be. (Sorry, Odyssey fans.)

Indeed, Lies of P fans have spent the last two years discussing their hopes for what a Wizard of Oz Soulslike might look like, with villains such as the flying monkeys, living trees and, of course, The Wicked Witch of the West. I'd like to see players take Toto down too.

"What if Dorothy needs to return to Oz to purge the corruption that Paracelsus has created?" wrote a fan in one of the various reddit threads discussing hopes for an Oz-based sequel, many of which date back a couple of years. "Paracelsus is clearly a deceiver — as was the Wizard of Oz, so they may be one and the same? Or he is continuing the work of the original Wizard of Oz and is the 'new' Wizard of Oz?"

We had a good time with Lies of P, awarding it 8/10 , while its subsequent expansion Overture also secured a 8/10. "Even if it’s clearly dancing on the same old strings, Lies of P: Overture is an excellent expansion that adds a whole lot more to a game that was already great."

articles.title: Live-Action Crazy Taxi Movie, New Sonic Animated Series, and Stranger Than Heaven Adaptation Heading to Netflix
articles.summary: Netflix has announced three Sega video game adaptations: a live-action comedy Crazy Taxi movie, a new Sonic animated series, and an adaptation of RGG Studio's yet to be released Stranger Than Heaven.
articles.body:
Netflix has announced three Sega video game adaptations: a live-action comedy Crazy Taxi movie, a new Sonic animated series, and a live-action movie adaptation of RGG Studio's yet to be released Stranger Than Heaven .

The Crazy Taxi movie is described as ‘live-action comedy,' and the Stranger Than Heaven adaptation is 'live-action crime.’ The new Sonic animation is obviously for kids.

Crazy Taxi comes first. It’s written by Dan Gregor and Doug Mand, the duo behind the 2025 reboot of The Naked Gun. Neal H. Moritz, Toby Ascher, and Toru Nakahara, the producers behind the Sonic franchise, are on board to produce.

“Great games already have what every adaptation is chasing — characters people love, worlds they know by heart, and fandoms that show up,” commented Brandon Riegg, VP of Nonfiction and Transmedia at Netflix. “With Crazy Taxi, Sonic, and Stranger Than Heaven, we get to work across three completely different eras of Sega’s catalog, celebrating everything fans love, while introducing them to new audiences.”

Shuji Utsumi, President and COO of Sega, added: "We've watched Netflix take on stories across every kind of format and treat each one with real craft, and seeing that same dedication applied to Sonic, Crazy Taxi, and Stranger Than Heaven is something we at Sega are incredibly proud to be a part of. The fandoms of these games deserve storytelling that honors what makes each title special, and we know Netflix shares that commitment. This is just the start of what these titles can become."

Toru Nakahara, Head Producer at Sega, told fans to expect “something cute yet cool” for Sonic, something “hilariously crazy” for Crazy Taxi, and a “badass action drama” for Stranger Than Heaven. Moritz and Ascher said of Crazy Taxi: “This film is for anyone who’s spent hours behind the wheel of a yellow cab on their Dreamcast, with the music cranked up, smashing through everything in sight just to make the next fare.”

The new animated series, currently in development with Carlos Stevens and Toru Nakahara, will present Sonic and his friends as heroes for an upper pre-school audience — a high-voltage, comedic, yet emotionally grounded series built for kids who want to feel a little edge, a little attitude, and a lot of “that’s my crew” wish fulfillment. Three seasons of Netflix’s Sonic Prime are also now available to stream only on Netflix.

And here’s the official line on Stranger Than Heaven:

From RGG Studio — developer of the Like a Dragon / Yakuza series — Stranger Than Heaven takes place in early 20th-century Japan, following a foreigner who claws his way from destitute stranger to feared yakuza to entertainment tycoon. Against the backdrop of a changing nation, how will he build an empire while balancing honor and betrayal? Details are under wraps, but a live-action film will bring a new lens to this epic world and franchise.

Netflix is all in on video game adaptations, and there’s a lot in the works. It’s got a live-action Assassin's Creed series, live-action Gears of War film, animated series adaptations based on Minecraft, Magic: The Gathering, and Clash of Clans, and Overcooked competition series; second seasons of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners and Splinter Cell: Deathwatch; and the third and final season of Devil May Cry. At BlizzCon 2026 over the weekend, Blizzard announced a Diablo animated series for Netflix , with talks ongoing for adaptations of Overwatch and Warcraft.

articles.title: Star Trek: Will the Saga of the Resurrected Captain Kirk End in Triumph or Tragedy?
articles.summary: IDW's critically acclaimed Star Trek: The Last Starship has reached its endgame. We chat with writers Collin Kelly and Jackson Lanzing to find out more about how it caps off the story of the resurrected James T. Kirk.
articles.body:
The Star Trek franchise may be in a bit of a weird place right now following the cancellation of Star Trek: Starfleet Academy and the impending end of Strange New Worlds , but never let it be said that there aren't great stories being told in this iconic sci-fi universe. Look no further than IDW's Star Trek: The Last Starship, a book that explores the aftermath of the horrific event known as The Burn. This series has seen the resurrection of Captain James T. Kirk in the 31st century, but can even a man as heroic as Kirk guide the Federation through its darkest hour? Is that even his goal anymore?

Everything in the series is coming to a head now as writers Collin Kelly and Jackson Lanzing prepare to wrap up their dramatic saga with The Last Starship #12 in October. It all comes down to the two driving forces of the series - Kirk and Captain Delacourt Sato - as they seek to put aside their differences and forge an alliance to save the galaxy from ruin.

First, check out an exclusive preview of Star Trek: The Last Starship #11 (due out on September 16), and then read on to learn more about how Kelly and Lanzing aim to cap off the series with a bang to rival that of The Burn itself.

Star Trek: The Last Starship #11 Preview Gallery

IGN: It was more than a little bittersweet to learn that the series is ending after 12 issues. Was it always the plan to come in and tell a leaner, more focused story than you did with Flagship?

Lanzing: Rest assured, it’s always been the plan.

Kelly: In our minds, 12 issues was always the target. The Last Starship was designed as a prestige maxi-series - four three-issue chapters that cover 100 years of the Burn. This was never meant to go forever - with Disco on the horizon, we even know how things will end up. But HOW it ends - that’s where our story lives, and that finale gives the entire story its shape.

Lanzing: The most important part of a story is its ending - and we’ve known the ending of TLS since before we wrote page 1.

IGN: So much of the series has revolved around the complex dynamic between Sato and Kirk. Has it been fun writing them as full-blown enemies in these recent issues? Are they going to be able to put aside their differences in the final arc?

Kelly: I know I just said that it wasn’t meant to go on forever, but that doesn’t mean we wouldn’t like to write these two forever, ESPECIALLY when they’re at odds. Two men, so alike but so different, who - in their conflict - bring out the best in one another, but through that conflict, make something incredible? After writing together for almost 20 years, that’s the kind of relationship that Jack and I have some affection for. Kirk and Sato are clashing furiously over the how and why …but when it comes to the what , to their shared drive to save the Federation, and preserve the legacy of all that makes Starfleet great - that’s something that will force the two men into alliance. And through that alliance…they will achieve something bold .

Lanzing: The conflict between Kirk and Sato is the center of the series, so of course turning that all the way up has been a total delight. They bring out both the best and the worst in each other - up until the very end.

IGN: The series has been relying on time dilation to push the story forward lately. Does that introduce extra challenges for you as writers dealing with such a tricky sci-fi narrative device?

Kelly: Absolutely, but it’s a challenge we signed up for. The time-dilation element of the story - while it’s mechanically a great way to assay the 100 years our tale takes place over - made its way into the narrative purely as a thought experiment: how does relativistic space travel function without the dilithium to magically foreshorten every distance? But more importantly - what are the emotional consequences for the crew? We wanted the Omega’s mission to take everything from its crew - and that includes every semblance of the lives they’ve known. Everyone they’ve ever loved “back home”, wherever that may be - by the time we hit Issue 11, those people are assuredly dead, or at least well close to dying. It has caused a lot of headaches on the narrative side, absolutely - but the pay off we get from the trauma it puts our characters through is well worth it.

Lanzing: It’s what makes this story unique in all of Star Trek, and it’s a challenge we’re really proud to have taken on.

IGN: At its core, The Last Starship is about exploring whether the Federation’s ideals can survive the galaxy’s darkest hour. Will we get a definitive answer to that question by the end?

Kelly: We’ve been writing Star Trek for over seven years for IDW - “can the ideals of the Federation survive” is a theme that we circle, over and over. It’s a question we’re all hungry for, because the ideals of the UFP are the ideals that so many of us want to see thrive in the real world. If Starfleet can face the worst of the universe and still make it, perhaps we can too.

Lanzing: Will you get a definitive answer? Yes. Issue Twelve is waiting.

You introduced the concept of the Emerald Chain as a mob-like protection racket in this post-Burn climate. Did you see that organization as the ultimate expression of everything the Federation isn’t?

Kelly: That’s a fun question, because…no, I don’t think the Chain is the Federation's opposite, any more than Klingons are humanity’s opposite. But a dark reflection? Absolutely. And that’s what’s particularly great about using them as our villain in this story, here at the seeming end of the Federation’s life. Because they’re not a massive hegemonic AI with the power of a god; they’re not aliens that exist outside of time; they’re capitalists. They’re liars and abusers and usurers, but they also understand that wealth comes from a system of exploitation, which means that the system must maintain populations to be exploited. They’re not evil…they’re selfish.

And ultimately, that’s the real enemy of the UFP, which is to say the enemy of Gene Roddenberry’s IDIC - Infinite Diversity in Infinite Combinations. If you care only about yourself and what you can gain, it’s impossible to celebrate the differences that make other people incredible. The Chain wants to lock us down; the Fed wants to lift us up. Being lifted - lifting - it takes far more effort…but it’s the only way to see the incredible things on the horizon.

IGN: I’m sure the two of you have more collaborations planned in general, but is there any chance we’ll see more Star Trek projects from you after The Last Starship #12?

Kelly: We’ve had an incredible time on Star Trek - genuinely, being trusted to tell these stories is one of the greatest high points of our career. But now, indeed, it’s time for us to cede the captains’ chairs to two new commanders - Christopher Cantwell and Charlie Jane Anders, both of whom have new flagship Star Trek books coming, both of which are INCREDIBLE - and step back to other projects that need our love. In November, we’re launching a new Dungeons & Dragons #1 from Dark Horse, and we have a creator owned horror series coming out through IDW Dark called You'll Never Leave This Place Alive.

Lanzing: Now, is that to say that you’ll never see us on a Star Trek comic again? I think we love it too much to stay away forever. There is still space for new stories in the The Last Starship-a-verse, even with the main plot concluded…

Kelly: …but truthfully? We hope the next time you see our name attached to Star Trek, it’ll be on TV.

Star Trek: The Last Starship #12 will be released on October 21, with a final order cutoff of September 14. You can preorder a copy at your local comic shop .

articles.title: The AOC 16" 1080p Portable USB Monitor For Laptop, Switch, or Gaming Handheld Drops to $49.99

articles.body:
It's no surprise why USB portable monitors are so popular. They provide extra screen real estate for laptop users and they're much slimmer and lighter than your average monitor so you can carry them around. Many newer laptops now have USB ports that can power the monitor so that you don't even need to plug it into an outlet. In addition to boosting productivity on a laptop, the monitor also works as a totable display for your Nintendo Switch. Talk about convenience!

AOC 15.6" 1080p USB-C Portable Monitor for $49.99

For a limited time, Amazon has dropped the price on the AOC 15.6" USB Portable Monitor (16T20) for just $49.99 with free shipping. The AOC 16T20 is a portable 15.6" monitor that weighs in at just 1.54 pounds and measures about 0.38" thin. It's small and slim enough to fit inside a laptop bag or backpack. It sports a sturdy metal frame and includes a smart cover that doubles as a kickstand. The 15.6" IPS display features a 1080p resolution (141ppi), 60Hz refresh rate, wide 178-degree viewing angle, and an anti-glare matte surface. It even has built-in speakers.

Connectivity options include two USB Type-C ports and one mini HDMI port to connect to a laptop, tablet, or handheld gaming PC for use as a main or secondary display. If your device is equipped with a USB Type-C output with Power Delivery, then a single cable can be used for both video and power. You will have to use the two-cable setup (one USB cable to the handheld, one USB cable to a wall charger) for this to work properly. The 1080p 60Hz panel best complements the Nintendo Switch, since the Switch only supports up to 720p @ 60Hz anyway. The Steam Deck and Switch 2 can support higher resolutions and refresh rates, but at that point you're really taxing your system, and 1080p/60Hz on a smaller display is an ideal balance between visual fidelity and playable framerates.

articles.title: The Steam Frame Was Probably Supposed to Cost About $750
articles.body:
Now that the Steam Frame is here, and we know it starts at $1,059 , it's clear that Valve had to raise the price a bit due to the ongoing RAM crisis.

Just like with the Steam Machine, I got a chance to sit down with Valve to talk about the Frame , and I was told by Valve Engineer Pierre-Loup Griffais that I could look at the price increases for the Steam Deck and Steam Machine to get a good idea of what the company was initially targeting for the VR headset. For reference, the Steam Deck got a massive price increase back in May, jumping to $789, up from $549. That's a pretty sizable 43% jump, or $240.

If the Steam Frame also saw its prices jump by around 43%, it's likely that the headset would have cost around $750, just like the Steam Machine. That would mean the Steam Frame now, due to higher hardware costs for memory and the Qualcomm chip that powers it, is around $310 more expensive than it would have been in the before-times.

Now, this is just napkin math, and I could very well be off the target here, but at that original price, the Steam Frame would have been a much more compelling headset, especially since the Meta Quest 3 hasn't yet had a major price increase. Meta's headset, after all, still starts at around $499.

Still, even at its current price, the Steam Frame is far from the most expensive PCVR headset on the market right now, especially when you compare it to other wireless headsets. Something like the Samsung Galaxy XR headset will cost you $1,899, and while it has much nicer OLED optics, it has a pretty similar SoC and RAM configuration.

Valve isn't alone it its higher-than-normal prices, either. Both the PS5 and Xbox Series X have had major price hikes this year, and pretty much every part of your gaming PC is going up in price, especially graphics cards , SSDs and RAM. It's unlikely that these high prices are going to go away anytime soon, either, as it looks like the memory manufacturing capacity for next year has already been sold through, largely to AI hyperscalers.

articles.title: Valve’s Steam Frame costs $1,059
articles.summary: Valve’s Steam Frame VR headset will start at $1,059, and the company has opened up a waitlist system for interested buyers.
articles.body: Valve is finally releasing its Steam Frame headset, which can run both flat and VR games locally and stream both kinds of games from your PC. The Steam Frame will start at $1,059. Valve will also offer a 1TB model that starts at $1,299. Every Steam Frame will come with a copy of Half-Life: Alyx, Valve’s made-for-VR entry in the Half-Life franchise, and Valve has ported the game to run natively on the headset as well as via streaming. Here are the prices for the Frame across several different currencies for the two configurations: * Steam Frame 256GB: $1,059 / $1,529 CAD / €1,049 / £889 / $1,609 AUD / 4,539 zlotys * Steam Frame 1TB: $1,299 / $1,859 CAD / €1,279 / £1,089 / $1,969 AUD / 5,549 zlotys [Media: Like with the Steam Machine, Valve will have a waitlist system for interested Steam Frame buyers, with a lottery for the first batch. Between now and September 17th at 10AM PT, you can sign up for the Steam Frame configuration you’d like to potentially buy. After that deadline, Valve will randomize the list, then tell buyers if they’ve won the lottery or will instead be added to the waitlist. If you’re chosen in the lottery, Valve should let you purchase on September 18th. If not, you can still join the waitlist. Once you get an offer to purchase a Steam Frame, you’ll have 72 hours to complete your order. If you want the least pressure on your face, my colleague Sean Hollister, who reviewed the headset, strongly recommends Valve’s ergonomic accessories kit, which comes with a removable top head strap that really helps the 1-pound headset float more comfortably, as well as a nose piece that blocks out more light for better immersion and a pair of “Knuckles”-style hand straps that can let you fully open and close your hands in VR games without dropping the controllers. There’s also an accessory replacement kit with replacement parts (with one face gasket, one head cushion, and one light blocker), and although the Frame doesn’t come with a USB-C charger, Valve is selling a separate one. Here are the prices for those extra accessories: * Ergonomic accessories kit: $59 / $89 CAD / €69 / £59 / $99 AUD / 279 zlotys * Accessory replacement kit: $49 / $69 CAD / €59 / £49 / $89 AUD / 229 zlotys * PSU (charger): $29 / $49 CAD / €39 / £29 / $49 AUD / 139 zlotys [Image: [Image: Additionally, Valve will be linking to one third-party accessory developed by a close partner: the Arcturus Vision Camera, a $149 accessory that plugs into the Steam Frame’s nose bridge port to give it color passthrough vision (the Frame has monochrome passthrough by default) and record spatial video. It’s a 5K60 10-bit HDR stereo camera that closely hugs the curve of the Steam Frame’s lens and switches the view to color the moment you plug it in. [Image: [Image: A 1080p screen capture of Sean’s backyard with and without the Arcturus Vision Camera while playing mixed reality title Cubism. The Arcturus provides much higher resolution than the screenshot shows. Images: Sean Hollister / The Verge Arcturus, which also helped Valve develop the computer vision systems it uses for all of the Frame’s headset tracking, says it’ll be careful not to ship the camera as soon as you order it, because the company knows not everyone will manage to get a confirmed Steam Frame preorder. “Launch orders will be held for several days to allow customers to coordinate with their Steam Frame orders,” it writes. And while we don’t have a date, price, or photo just yet, Valve designers Joy Lyons and Jeremy Selan tell The Verge they’ll launch an additional modular “enthusiast kit” that changes out the Steam Frame’s entire head strap, battery, and audio solution for one that lets you stack a second magnetic battery onto the first one to double the Frame’s battery capacity, a premium set of off-ear floating speakers based on the Valve Index Ear Speakers, and additional eye spacers that can get you even closer to (or farther from) its lenses. Valve first revealed the Steam Frame alongside the new Steam Controller and Steam Machine late last year, and while it initially expected to launch the headset sometime in early 2026, the release was pushed back due in part to RAMageddon. The company ended up releasing the products over the course of the past several months, starting first with the Steam Controller in May, then the Steam Machine in June, and now the Steam Frame.

articles.title: The Steam Frame is made for irresponsible hardware nerds like me
articles.summary: The Steam Frame, Valve’s new wearable computer, is about more than virtual reality. Here’s our review.
articles.body: For nearly three weeks, I’ve been testing the limits of Valve’s Steam Frame, the company’s new wearable PC. At first glance, it’s easy to write it off as a pricey headset that missed the VR craze. At $1,059 with 256GB of storage or $1,299 for 1TB, it costs two to three times as much as similar-looking headsets from Meta. You should not write it off that way. The Steam Frame isn’t just a VR headset. It’s not even primarily a VR headset. And it’s the most comfortable headset I’ve ever worn. It weighs just over 1 pound (469g) with its optional top head strap attached, and doesn’t leave a mark on my face even after hours of use. The Steam Frame is far more ambitious than VR alone. It’s an experimental attempt at a complete spatial computer that you can wear, not unlike the Apple Vision Pro, only here it’s aimed at gamers who want to play their flat library of Steam games plus the handful of VR titles on tap. [Image: Pictured with optional $59 kit with hand straps and top third head strap; I highly recommend them. No, if you write off the Steam Frame, it should be because you don’t want to pay $1,000-plus for early access hardware. Every day I spend with the Steam Frame, I feel like a beta tester. I’ve seen games crash so hard I needed to reboot the headset. I’ve had virtual objects, controls, and audio disappear. I’ve seen the entire device lose power more than once, its screen winking out right in front of my eyes. But you should know I’m having so much fun. The Frame’s so comfortable that I don’t mind wearing it, and it feels like one of the most exciting betas I’ve ever tried. Like the Steam Deck at its debut, this is gadget nerd wish fulfillment. It’s a chance to watch Valve, one of the most intriguing companies in gaming, build a plane while flying it. [Product: Steam Frame | The Steam Frame is primarily a gaming device. And it can certainly play games in a lot of different ways: * It can stream any flat or VR game from your Steam-equipped desktop or laptop. * It can play less demanding Windows games via emulation on its Arm-based Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 chip. * It can effectively be a Meta Quest, playing immersive VR games originally designed for Meta’s Android-based headsets. * It can play games natively designed for the Steam Frame’s Linux-on-Arm, too — like a new standalone version of the best single-player VR game, 2020’s Half-Life: Alyx. * And it can play mixed reality games where virtual objects seemingly float in your real world, as seen through the headset’s passthrough cameras. It can do much of this because of the power of software — because Valve has spent years making games run where they didn’t originally belong. [Media: But that’s just what it can do with games. I am typing these words to you from virtual reality. I’m inside the Steam Frame surrounded by six virtual screens. In front of me is Google Docs on effectively the largest computer monitor I’ve ever used, even counting the 48-inch TV that once lived atop my desk, and that screen is not alone. If I spin my office chair to the left, I’m facing my notes, calendar, and web browser. Spin it to the right, and there’s The Verge’s newsroom, my email, and a panel of Steam games. Above me, a Linux copy of Space Cadet Pinball waits to be played, while a YouTube window pipes in lo-fi music to help me focus. Three of these screens are copies of my desktop PC’s three monitors, streaming from that PC, while the other three are running on the headset itself. I have Windows and Linux desktops running side by side in my own private world. But whenever I try to explore all the possibilities I’ve just laid out, I quickly run into unexpected limitations, crashes, and bugs. [Image: A peek at my multi-monitor Windows desktop inside the Steam Frame. Let’s say I’m on my living room couch, and I want to stream a game from my PC that won’t easily run on the headset’s own chip, like the just-released Star Wars: Zero Company. The headset gives me a choice: I can launch the game in a window, or I can stream my entire PC desktop to the device. I launch it in a window, then use the virtual laser pointers in Valve’s wand controllers to stretch the screen across my entire living room wall, while my wife sits next to me watching the BTS concert on my much smaller real-life TV on the same wall. I click the grip button on Valve’s wands one more time, and they begin emulating a full Xbox gamepad, with every button I need to play. [Image: Valve’s virtual laser pointers are the primary way to navigate the UI; the headset can’t track your hands without the wands yet. But suddenly, my streaming game is lagging and dropping frames like nobody’s business — because the Frame couldn’t decide whether to prioritize my home Wi-Fi or Valve’s included 6GHz wireless dongle, the company tells me later. My favorite seat on the living room couch is only about 12 feet and one wall away from the dongle, but that’s apparently the edge of its useful range. While Valve has “multi-link” streaming tech that could let the Frame balance both connections simultaneously, it currently only works when you’re streaming your entire PC. Shall I try streaming my entire PC to the Steam Frame instead? But now I no longer feel like I’m hanging out with my wife, because the Frame’s passthrough cameras only work with streaming windows, not entire streaming PCs. The wands don’t work as a gamepad when streaming entire PCs, either. Nor do my Bluetooth keyboard and mouse when I pair them to the Frame. Back in my virtual office, where I’m surrounded by six virtual screens, the same limitation means I don’t get to control them all simultaneously. I have to use my desktop mouse and keyboard to control the Windows screens, and my Steam Frame’s controls to control the Linux ones. The wands’ laser pointers can thankfully cross these boundaries, but sometimes I’ll click and nothing will happen. When I try adding a seventh virtual screen, the Steam Frame chokes, and everything — all seven screens and the device’s entire user interface — spontaneously disappears. None of the buttons on my wands bring the UI back, so it’s time for a reboot again. I’m not angry, and I don’t expect it’ll stay this way for long. But we can only review what’s in the box, and these are the kinds of things reviewers are currently experiencing. [Image: When I set streaming aside and try playing games on its own Qualcomm chip, the Steam Frame has more power than I expect. There’s enough that I’d happily play VR games like Half-Life: Alyx from beginning to end on this device — fan-made Alyx mods are natively supported, too! — and I found myself getting sucked back into all kinds of lightweight flat games like Dave the Diver, Blue Prince, and Streets of Rage 4. In terms of flat-screen gaming performance, it currently feels less powerful than the aging Steam Deck, with welterweight games like Hi-Fi Rush at the very edge of what I’m comfortable playing on its Qualcomm chip. But here, I’m not constrained by a single 7-inch handheld screen, or even my 65-inch OLED TV. I’m backstabbing buddies in Super Battle Golf on a screen the size of my entire living room wall — while chatting with them in Discord on a second virtual screen that contains a full Linux desktop. My Steam Deck handheld tops out at 1280 x 800 resolution, and by default, Valve locks flat Steam Frame games to a similar 1280 x 720. But the Frame’s LCD panels actually provide 2160 x 2160 per eye, and you can cram an incredible number of gaming pixels into that space if you try. The Frame can manage a game as old as 2007’s Portal at 2.8K resolution on a movie theater-sized virtual screen. There’s even a 5120 x 2880 option, though I haven’t found a single game weak enough to run that way. [Image: The Frame controllers have every button, joystick, and trigger an Xbox gamepad does, in addition to VR controls. Eye-tracking can help. By taking advantage of a technique called foveated rendering, games like Half-Life: Alyx and Dungeons of Eternity can spend more of their processing power producing sharp images where you’re actually looking while reducing resolution where you’re not. Dungeons of Eternity let me adjust the effect enough to tell it’s making a real difference. Red Matter 2 claims it’s providing an effective 4096 x 4096 resolution to my retinas, and I don’t doubt it: There’s a computer monitor early in the game whose glass screen is covered in lifelike scratches, and it looks incredible. [Image: A flat 1080p screenshot really does not do it justice. The Steam Frame doesn’t have dedicated Netflix or YouTube apps, but DRM content appears to work fine in the Chromium web browser: I’ve been watching full episodes of Peaky Blinders on Netflix almost every day at lunch. YouTube works in the browser (though not YouTube VR), and you can download VLC to watch all kinds of local video files. Speaking of streaming, you can stream your entire Sony PS5 to the Steam Frame with the Asobi app — I played some Yakuza that way. [Image: [Image: And if you’re nerd enough to have 3D Blu-ray rips like me, Skybox is one of the excellent video players that’ll let you watch them in glorious 3D with convincing surround sound. Into the Spider-Verse looked amazing from my seat in a virtual movie theater, even though Steam Frame’s LCD displays don’t have the rich color of OLED. And Valve’s quad drivers sound remarkably good for something built into the frame of a headset. But as of today, it’s tough to tell whether any given standalone app or game will run on the Steam Frame’s Arm chip — and run well — until you spend hours and gigabytes downloading and trying it for yourself. [Image: You can even edit images in GIMP on the Linux desktop if you really want to. Many just do, and it never ceases to wow me when I fire up, say, Fallout: New Vegas and the game actually launches on an entirely different operating system atop an entirely different processor architecture than its developers imagined. But some will launch and then take ages to load, like Shadow of the Tomb Raider, or fail to produce a visible image even though I can hear the game’s music, like Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time, or throw a major error on launch, like Doom: The Dark Ages. Like with the Steam Deck, Valve will try to warn you first: It has a compatibility review program, badges for “Verified” and “Unsupported” games, and a dedicated “Great on Frame” store page so you can buy titles that should just work. But the program’s in its infancy with just 130 “Verified” titles at the time I write the words, and even the badge is no guarantee a game will play perfectly. I was having a blast hacking and slashing skeletons in the Valve-verified Dungeons of Eternity for hours on end — but near the end of one dungeon, I suddenly lost audio and the ability to swing my club with my right controller. When I tried to throw my club at foes, it would just vanish. [Image: The Steam Frame’s passthrough vision is monochrome, not color, though I’ll show you an accessory later that changes that. Valve’s Jeremy Selan, one of the Steam Frame’s developers, suggests it won’t always be this way — I won’t always have to think about architectures and streaming technologies. I won’t always be bumping up against the seams. “Our goal is that even though there’s a variety of ways to have these two computers talk to each other, we don’t want the user to have to think about ‘Am I streaming 2D? Am I streaming VR? Where are my controllers paired?’ We want every possible scenario to just work,” he says. “We’re going to try to make it where the device is just fun and seamless and you don’t have to think about those little things.” He says I will “absolutely” be able to use the Steam Frame controllers as a gamepad for my entire remote PC, for example. That feature is already on the way and might even arrive by the time you read these words. And he takes a moment to thank me for my bug reports. “No hyperbole: On my computer right now are the things you just mentioned, and those are my tasks for the next week.” He points out that Valve has already fixed a weird green line I saw underneath my streaming windows, and added the ability to make floating windows curved instead of flat, just two days after I asked for that. [Image: I make almost all my windows curved, since they look crisper through the headset that way. Selan admits that Valve does rely on early adopters to find issues, because the company’s own engineers “have become our own worst playtesters” after working on the headset for years. But he says that the way Valve works is to ship hundreds of updates to address user feedback. That’s what it did with the original Steam Controller and Steam Deck, and that’s what it sounds like he’s planning here. I can’t think of a single company that’s ever supported hardware this way, but the Steam Deck went from a glorious mess to the easiest handheld gaming PC to recommend. Valve is still adding new features years later. And Valve has unified its software releases, so the Steam Machine (and soon Steam Frame) gets many of the same improvements. The top feature he’d like to add to the Steam Frame is hand-tracking, he says, which is already working under the hood. (The controllers do per-finger sensing so you can have convincing virtual hands in games, but you can’t yet drop the wands and use your real hands instead.) And he’d like to get the Steam Machine streaming to the Steam Frame, a feature that won’t be available at launch. “But we don’t get to work on those fun things until we make the device a joy for people who are new to it like yourself,” he tells me. Valve wants the bug reports to keep coming in. [Image: [Image: If I’m being honest, I originally thought I’d spend most of this review comparing the Steam Frame to Meta’s Quest 3 and Quest 3S and the Apple Vision Pro. I figured I’d be talking about pancake versus Fresnel lenses, battery life, game selection, the fact that Valve’s headset doesn’t come with color passthrough cameras despite costing two to three times as much, the fact that Meta’s software is far more fleshed out. [Image: Valve’s battery is small but makes for a comfortable curved rear headpiece, and I can route an external battery to it easily. But here’s the simple truth: I don’t want to wear a Meta Quest or an Apple Vision Pro, because comfort trumps all. I own a Quest 2 and have access to the rest, but they all collect dust unless there’s a truly epic game to play — because they’re all front-heavy and put unwanted pressure on my face. When it comes to comfort, the Steam Frame mops the floor with anything else I’ve tried. It doesn’t leave a red ring around my face. In fact, it can float so freely on my face that I don’t need to keep the Frame’s silky cushions attached — I can remove the rear one for less bulk against pillows and headrests, a trick that Selan says he sometimes uses in bed. (The optional top head strap is part of a $59 accessories kit, though it also includes Valve’s excellent “Knuckles”-style hand straps and so I think it’s worth the money.) The only thing I find uncomfortable about the Frame is that it gets warm enough to trigger an audible fan, but at least it’s a tolerable “whoosh” sound (not a whine) and it keeps my face cool by sending in fresh air. --- Ask me anything! Do you have a burning question about the Steam Frame that I didn’t answer in this review? I’m holding a subscriber-only AMA at 4PM ET today (that’s 1PM PT for me!). If you get your questions in early, I might even be able to test new things for you! --- And while the Frame’s 21.6-watt-hour battery doesn’t last long — heavy games can last less than an hour, and I’ve yet to see more than two hours in its battery-saving mode or while streaming — its rear-mounted USB-C port is well placed to route a cable down to a battery in my pocket. Even my tiny 36Wh Iniu battery gave me an entire extra hour of play, and my old 100Wh HyperJuice battery lasted an entire 2.5-hour session of Dungeons of Eternity while charging up the Steam Frame, too. You can effortlessly add color passthrough to the Frame if you want, by the way — Arcturus, which helped build the Frame’s entire vision system, is now selling a perfect-fit 5K60 10-bit HDR stereo camera for $150. Just shove it into the Frame’s nose bridge port and the headset’s monochrome passthrough vision automatically changes to color, because Valve baked in native support. It’s clear enough that I can read my phone’s screen, something you can’t do without, and it lets you record spatial video clips. [Image: [Image: That said, Valve’s stock infrared camera system has charm — when I need a glass of water in the middle of the night, it’s fun to walk around with what’s effectively a night vision headset on. The Arcturus camera isn’t the only modular component coming for the Steam Frame, by the way. The entire compute core of the Frame is detachable so you can connect it to other head strap, audio, and battery solutions instead, and Valve is planning one of its own: An “Enthusiast Kit” will come with a new head strap that lets you stack a second magnetic battery pack onto the first one to double the Frame’s battery capacity, a premium set of off-ear floating speakers based on the Valve Index Ear Speakers, and additional eye spacers that can get you even closer to (or farther from) its lenses. No price, release date, or photos of that one just yet. [Image: I can’t imagine the Steam Frame will be anywhere near as much of a success as the Steam Deck. It costs so much more, and it requires people to wear a gadget on their face. That’s why most of these headsets have always been a hard sell. But the Frame doesn’t cost quite as much as I feared it might, and it finally lets game developers target a consumer wireless headset that isn’t ultimately controlled by Mark Zuckerberg, or any of the other companies that tried headsets but don’t seem to care as much anymore. But even if you don’t want to play VR games, even if you believe VR is dead for now, there are all kinds of intriguing things to do with a Linux desktop and a catalog of flat-screen Steam games on your head. If you’re the kind of nerd who’d love that, I don’t want to scare you away. The Steam Deck was a mess at launch, but it was also so much fun. Sometimes becoming a beta tester isn’t such a bad thing.
