articles.title: Steam Frame – The Valve Interview
articles.summary: Now that the Steam Frame is finally here, Valve's entire hardware lineup is now out in the wild. I got a chance to sit down with Valve software developers Pierre-Loup Griffais and Jeff Leinbaugh to talk about the new VR headset, and it sounds like the launch is only the beginning for the Steam Frame. Because while it is more expensive than something like the Meta Quest 3, Valve is hopeful that as an open platform, the Frame is going to be able to evolve over time, and who knows what it's going to be capable of a couple years down the line.
articles.body:
Now that the Steam Frame is finally here, Valve's entire hardware lineup is officially out in the wild. I got a chance to sit down with Valve software developers Pierre-Loup Griffais and Jeff Leinbaugh to talk about the new VR headset, and it sounds like the launch is only the beginning for the Steam Frame. Because while it is more expensive than something like the Meta Quest 3, Valve is hopeful that as an open platform, the Frame is going to be able to evolve over time, and who knows what it's going to be capable of a couple years down the line.

IGN: Why not have the option to have a wired connection from the PC to the Steam Frame?

Jeff Leinbaugh: Yeah, so the goal for the Steam Frame was a wireless experience, really to get over a massive use case friction hump. We've been working on that for a long time. We've been shipping updates and supporting Steam Link for VR for a bunch of other headsets as we've worked on that technology. And then the dongle, the adapter was the next step for that, because as you know, wireless networking setups vary a lot. So the adapter's a way to say, okay, this is the minimum bar, it’s in the box and is something that we can do a lot to ensure works pretty well.

So we see the Steam Frame as a streaming first headset, which for us, we think for the majority of people using it means a wireless streaming VR headset. We do have a [wired] mode that's still restricted behind the developer toggle, but it's something that's being worked on with a USB cable, if you've got a long enough USB cable to the PC, that can be used to stream and it augments the existing wireless adapter or other connections with multilink the same way that all of them work together.

Pierre-Loup Griffais: In general our goal, our aim is for the wireless adapter to be sufficient and that you shouldn't have to change your network configuration.

IGN: If the Steam Frame is designed to be streaming first, why not release a version with less RAM and a weaker chip to keep the price down, especially now that the RAM crisis has grown so bad?

Griffais: I think at this point, things were a little bit too far in development to fully rethink the product.

I would say that despite being streaming first, the ability to run things locally has been pretty well used in our observation and play testing, and I think there's some potential there to improve the experience even further. And so I think we're pretty happy with the trade-offs that we made along the way there to have both of those sides of the experience represented. And we expect that every user is going to approach it in a different way, where streaming might work best for a bunch of them, but standalone play would also work really well for some people.

Leinbaugh: Yeah, and that identity may evolve over time because we're still in the early phases of getting compatibility verification and all of that going, just like we were in the very early days of the Steam Deck. So as the number of standalone certified titles grows, people may see this as less of a primary streaming headset, depending on what they want to do. Some people may be content with one kind of gameplay, one way of playing it, other people may come in from the other side. So we're trying to improve all those angles.

IGN: Can you talk a little bit about the process of getting Proton compatibility running on ARM?

Griffais: Definitely. So the way that things run on the headset, Proton is the same exact Proton that you're used to on Steam Deck and Steam Machine and other platforms, but it's rebuilt natively for ARM instead. So all the Proton code is native for the platform. So as soon as the game exits the WIN 32 API environment and it's on the ARM native side, there's no performance hit from the ARM translation from that point on. So a lot of the code that powers the experience is actually Native ARM when you're running a game through Proton. But to achieve the emulation on the x86 side of things, we're using a program called FEX, which is a translation layer between x86 and ARM. We actually kicked off FEX development more than eight years ago at this point, thinking that it would be useful for things like that around this time.

So there's been a lot of work that went into it and integrating into Proton, making it work for Linux native games and so on. But given all that, we're at a point where compatibility is pretty much similar to what you're used to on Steam Deck. And a lot of the games that work to the same extent just with the performance difference because the GPU architecture is a little bit different and the ARM translation incurs some different performance characteristics on the CPU as well.

I would say also there's been a lot of work on the graphics driver side of things to make the driver able to run desktop-like games that are translated from DirectX 11, DirectX 12, as typically the drivers on those mobile chip sets, that's not their primary aim. But thanks to the open source nature of the drivers on Linux and Mesa, we've been able to do a ton of first party work there and improve it greatly.

IGN: Back when I visited in November, Valve was iffy on whether or not the Frame would be able to run Half-Life: Alyx natively, and now it works great. Do you think that performance is going to improve further as drivers mature?

Griffais: I think for Alyx specifically, if any work is left there on the performance side, it's going to be on the application side to make some final tweaks. But as we go doing that, we sometimes do new features in the driver or tweaks in the driver to accommodate that. But at this point, I think a lot of the performance has been tapped into, but it's possible we might discover some new untapped way of optimizing things further. There's been a ton of work that's been happening in tandem between the people working on Half-Life: Alyx optimization for the Frame and the driver, and a lot of those learnings actually will help other games, as well as help people tweak their games to run natively on Frame.

Leinbaugh: Yeah, going through the process of making Alyx run standalone is also helping us figure out the new problem of, "How do we make sure that VR games running standalone are a good experience?" Because we now are pretty good at getting non-VR games to run through Proton and making sure that those are verified and being comfortable with what those thresholds are.

For VR, it's kind of a different story because comfort is a bigger factor. So as we've gone through the process of making Alyx run better, we're learning about what's important when we look at other VR games to make sure that we can guarantee this is a good experience without setting a bar that's just unreasonably high, but something that's really useful to people who are using that as a tool to figure out what they should play. And one goal we have is, if we can lower the requirements on a game because we have driver improvements, re-projection improvements, that we're confident we'll still make that a good experience, then that's something that we would do as well once the technology for that is improved. We're pretty confident having a game like Alyx to test a lot of that stuff against has been really useful too.

IGN: Coming in at $1,059 makes sense in the current hardware landscape, but the elephant in the room is the Meta Quest 3 at around half the price. What sets the Steam Frame apart from Meta’s headsets?

Griffais: I think there's a bunch of different facets there. I mean, in practice, generally when we think about our products and what we want to bring to the table, we're not really directly comparing it to any other platform. We're trying to make choices that we think make sense for Steam users and will improve their experience playing a bunch of games. But for sure, I think our users, there's probably a bunch of use cases around modding and installing third party apps and things that we think Frame will work pretty well with.

And we're also very happy with the comfort, the weight of it, and the quality of the optics that you get for that. But as far as the price goes, I think it's a direct representation of the hardware that's in there, and there's not a lot of work that we're doing to try and muddy the picture there.

We're just building it for the cost that the parts in there cost us, and then passing that on to users as we're doing with other hardware.

IGN: When the Steam Frame was first revealed, we heard that Valve was trying to keep the price under the Index. How much has the RAM crisis moved up the price over what it theoretically was back then?

Griffais: Yeah, if you look at other comparable products like the Steam Deck or Steam Machine and what we were looking for originally and where it landed, it's kind of a similar price difference. It's really a reflection of the price changes in the market as a whole and the conditions around both things like, of course, memory and storage costs, but also even things like the main board cost, the layers of the main board itself, the copper, shipping… Everything is more expensive than it was this time last year. So all of that stuff comes into play there.

IGN: How much have the higher prices this year affected the demand for products like the Steam Deck and Steam Machine? How well did the Steam Machine sell?

Griffais: It's a little hard to say because we're still working on getting the whole launch quantity through, but in practice, I mean I think price for sure impacts demand. We'll have to monitor how things are going, but we're pretty comfortable with the fact that all these products are trending similarly to other products in the market. So for something, the Frame or a Steam Deck, of course, the value is a little bit harder to pinpoint compared to other PCs in the market because they have different aspects that they're bringing to play. The Deck’s portable platform, the Frame being the virtual reality form factor with the optics and a few things that are not really represented in the larger PC market.

But if you look at the memory and anything that has a similar amount of memory, it's kind of trending the same direction and Steam Machine is not really getting more expensive than a comparable PC. They're kind of evolving at the same spot in the same market, and I think the same will apply to the Frame as well.

IGN: Has the current hardware shortage impacted the way Valve is thinking about actually putting a Steam Deck 2 into development?

Griffais: Not really. I think the same way that we're working back from the user experience and what we're bringing to the table in terms of the same things that we've talked about before about how we want to make sure there's a very delineated performance improvement for something like a future Steam Deck, I think we're still looking at it in the same way.

It's just a matter of looking at the current conditions and seeing how and when we can deliver something like that. But from what we're working on as far as the user experience goes and what the product that we're trying to build goes, it's very similar goals.

IGN: The Valve Index launched with Half-Life: Alyx. Why launch the Steam Frame, especially at its price, without any new game?

Leinbaugh: Yeah, a huge part of our focus with this, because we were bringing our VR product line into SteamOS and Proton and game compatibility and everything that brings, we really prioritized getting software compatibility in a good state so that there would be a huge number of games, I mean as big as possible, available to play on the device or stream to the device on day one. And that's kind of the maximum value proposition that we saw with this, that you've got a lot of games to play and a lot of options of what games to play, even if they're VR games or not VR games. And so that's kind of what we're bringing to the launch.

IGN: When using the Steam Frame, I noticed that the default light seal wasn’t great, but the one included in the Ergonomic Accessories Kit was so much better. Why not include the larger light seal with the Steam Frame?

Griffais: I think the thing you just said about it having a real cost that's tangible I think is part of the picture there, because some of these accessories are not going to be used by everyone. So we wanted to make sure that we didn't burden the cost of the base offering for folks that didn't immediately need the different shape accessories for the face gaskets and things like the hand drops if they're not playing with that. So it's really a factor of trying to reduce it to the strict minimum that we saw most people would have a good experience with, and then for folks that need more to have it available separately.

IGN: I love how lightweight and comfortable the Steam Frame is, but the battery life isn’t very long. Are there any plans to sell an extra battery pack or any battery accessories?

Leinbaugh: No specific plans to talk about, but we've been thinking a lot about battery life. We thought a lot about the battery when we were deciding what to ship with the product, because like you said, weight is a big factor, and the bigger the battery is, the more you trade off a lot of other aspects of the experience.

So what we aimed for was something that was pretty balanced that would get you one to two hours of gameplay. And then we also have included some knobs to let people tweak that if they want to try to extend the battery life a little further, or if they're near a power source and they want to go full out and use the battery up faster, that's also an option. As far as charging, a lot of off-the-shelf battery banks and things, anything that does USB power delivery, 45 watts is a good target.

I think you can actually charge it faster than it'll drain if you go down to 20-ish watts, but it'll support 45 watts and that'll charge up really quickly from a battery bank or from a wall charger. But beyond that, we've been looking into what we could bring in the future as an alternate option for the strap because we designed the core and the strap modularly.

Everything that's in the strap, the audio, the strap itself, and the battery are things that potentially could be replaced in the future. One of those things that we're looking at is a potential strap that would offer a larger battery or hot swappable battery solution so that we could maybe deliver a first party version of something like that. At the same time, we're looking at alternate audio solutions, which all came up during the development of the product, but kind of like with the battery, they were not a good fit for the kind of baseline lightweight experience we thought would be most valuable to most people.

So we're also looking at what it would take to do an Index-style off-ear audio solution, and so we're kind of excited about exploring that and seeing if we can make something like that.

IGN: Do you envision third party manufacturers coming up with their own accessories to augment the Steam Frame with?

Leinbaugh: Yeah, we hope so. We have one partner already for the front port with the RGB cameras. And yeah, the port is good for more than just that potentially, so it really depends what people want to try, and yeah, we're excited about it.

IGN: How is Nvidia driver support coming along on SteamOS?

Griffais: Yeah, we're working on it hard. It's definitely at the top of our list. It's one of those things just like FEX and working on the Qualcomm driver, it just takes years. And so we've been at it for a few years already. The team is growing. We've done a few things like we've enabled the driver now in the main tree of SteamOS, so you can get things to light up on certain generations, but in terms of the performance difference between that driver and where the state of the art is, there's definitely still a little bit of a rift that we're trying to work on, but it's getting better day-to-day, so we're really hoping that at some point we can recommend it to users running that hardware, but right now it's still work in progress.

IGN: I’ve been using the Frame to stream 2D games a lot, how do y’all use it? Are you more VR focused or do you spend more time playing 2D games on a private screen?

Leinbaugh: I've gone back and forth a lot. I think the thing that I like to do has changed depending on what I'm playing. I went a couple months where I was mostly just playing local 2D content on the headset, and I was working on that a lot, and so I was playtesting it a lot, and basically that was the primary way I used it. But yeah, I'll notice something that I want to play in VR on PC, and then I'll get into a mode where I'm going home every night and streaming a Sim game or something in VR. Yeah, I don't think I have a consistent answer that would remain true for more than two to four weeks over the last year with how I've been using it. I know a lot of people in the team are different.

Some people have rarely used it to play VR games. Some people only use it as a VR headset playing with their PC and haven't done anything else. We don't want to tell people how to use it, because people even on the team have found value in these little corners of what it can do. So our goal has just been to pick a game and play it, and hopefully you don't have to think too hard about how you're getting into it or what's happening to put the game in front of you, but just to support all of those things, because we've seen how valuable it is to approach it from all those angles.

Griffais: Yeah, lately I've been playing Metal Gear Solid 4 on it and locally it runs really well. But the fact that I can have it, like you said, in the giant theater and also have a chat window open on the side or something is interesting and opens a lot of different possibilities. Personally, I really enjoy the fact that I can recline on my chair and leave my arms by my side while I'm playing a game like that instead of engaging my shoulders and always gripping a [standard] controller like that, so it's a little bit more relaxing.

But beyond that, when I was playing, I recently did a new play through Alyx because I was helping test and tweak the game there leading up to launch, and I found myself alternating between streaming and local. So I was streaming when no one was on the Machine because I could just use it for streaming, but then when someone was playing on there or someone was watching TV or something, I would just do a span of it playing locally, and being able to flip back and forth there was very valuable.

IGN: Speaking of the Machine, when will support for streaming to the Steam Frame from the Steam Machine be officially supported?

Griffais: I think we have a specific timeline. The core elements are all there in terms of getting the actual link up and running and all that. It's really things around the user experience and setting up the wireless adapter and all that that are still a work in progress. So in terms of the core experience, if you know how to set things up right now, you can get into it and get to the actual streaming and have no problems there, but it's not in a state where we would really recommend people do that because there's a set of paper cuts on the way in and out of that experience. So we're really hoping we can improve that around launch.

IGN: I was surprised by how much 2D streaming to the Frame changed the way I played games. What are some future possibilities you’re excited to see from the Steam Frame?

Griffais: I think beyond, I mean, it's kind of a tangent, but I'm personally also excited to see how people improve the experience beyond just 2D streaming, because there's some opportunities for augmenting 2D streaming in a way that I don’t really do with a flat screen. At some point, there was an industry push for stereo displays, 3D vision and a lot of things like that, but all those games I think would actually work pretty well streamed to a headset because you could have that effect because the display is stereo capable in that context. And so I'm really looking forward to seeing if people do more with that, because the idea that you could actually augment your game by streaming it in a way like that and not just merely have a big screen is pretty fascinating to me.

Griffais: Well, just if a game used to have stereo support, you could actually enable that 3D effect on a flat game, and I think that's pretty untapped at this point.

Leinbaugh: Yeah, and we've seen VR mod conversions before – that's not a new thing, but it's interesting when you have a device that can play a game anywhere along that spectrum from a flat screen game playing in a rectangle in a theater view all the way up to a full immersive VR with motion controls. Any kind of feature-add along that spectrum is something that you could test and try, and there might be value there when it makes really no difference that you just load it up and you may get stereo separation or depth or something. Those are all kinds of interesting options.

Griffais: A game developer could just do a minimal kind of addition, which is just putting their HUD out of the game when you're playing on a streaming setup like that or something equally light touch, but actually would change the experience quite a bit when you're on Frame.

IGN: It sounds like there are all kinds of possibilities on how the Steam Frame could evolve in the future. Do you see the Steam Frame as a fully-fleshed-out device or an early-adopter kind of product, where people should get it to look forward to future updates?

Leinbaugh: I mean, neither. Somewhere in the middle. We like getting excited about future possibilities for sure, and a lot of people do too, but that's not something you have to get excited about to go out and use Steam Frame. When we decided to make this and ship it, we did that because this was something that you could play your game library with and have fun with, and there's value there now. So I don't think it requires some assumption that you're investing in a future update or future tech.

And that's good for us because we can deliver something that we're confident that has a value and people will like now. But then we also get to watch what people like about it and read feedback for what people don't like. And then that can drive us to do those future updates that we're already excited about working on.

Griffais: I think a lot of those cool elements will actually come from the community as well. And I'm super excited to see what people do with that. It's kind of a canvas that's differently shaped than anything else that's been done before in terms of open platforms, like the possibilities that you can have to extend a Linux desktop into VR, or mod games into VR and into those hybrid things that we just discussed. There's a ton of possibilities there and we're super excited to see what people do with it. But I do think it's a pretty fully formed offering as is. You don't need any of that. You have access to your whole Steam library, you have the streaming core experience, you have local VR, all that stuff that you're talking about is there at launch. So I think there's not really an expectation that there's a missing piece that someone will fill in later.

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: Valve Says RAM Crisis Hasn’t Affected Plans for Steam Deck 2
articles.summary: It might be a worry that the ongoing RAM crisis would impact Valve’s plans for a device so sensitive to component costs like the Steam Deck 2. Thankfully, Valve says its plans haven’t changed.
articles.body:
It’s no secret that Valve is “hard at work” on Steam Deck 2 – its devs have said as much every time I’ve asked that question over the last several years, and their plans for a sequel have been clear from the start .

The crux of the message has always been that Valve is waiting for the proper technology in order to present a true “generational leap” in performance. The unspoken part of that, of course, is that Valve is waiting for not just the right level of performance, but the correct performance to price ratio that would make Steam Deck 2 a viable product.

In the time since the Steam Deck originally launched, a number of other, more powerful handheld gaming PCs have come to market – all at moderate to significantly higher prices. In other words, the performance might be there now, but the price isn’t.

It might be a worry, then, that the RAM crisis that has driven up hardware prices – everything from graphics cards to gaming consoles to the Steam Deck itself – would impact Valve’s plans for a device so sensitive to component costs like the Steam Deck 2.

Thankfully, Valve says its plans haven’t changed. My colleague Jackie recently sat down with Valve software developers Pierre-Loup Griffais and Jeff Leinbaugh, and they had a reassuring answer to her question about whether the ongoing RAM shortage has impacted Valve’s plans.

“Not really,” said Griffais. “We've talked before about how we want to make sure there's a very delineated performance improvement for something like a future Steam Deck, and I think we're still looking at it in the same way.

“It's just a matter of looking at the current conditions and seeing how and when we can deliver something like that. But from what we're working on, as far as the user experience goes and what the product that we're trying to build goes, it's very similar goals.”

To me, that sounds like Valve’s target hasn’t changed, but the timeline might have. As I said before, it’s all about finding the right price to performance ratio where a new Steam Deck would make sense.

On the other hand, the Steam Machine and Steam Frame have shown that Valve isn’t afraid of simply passing higher component prices along to the consumer. But given that Steam Deck demand has reportedly cratered due to its ballooned price, up to $789 for the 512GB OLED model that previously cost $549, I have to assume that Valve is in no hurry to push out an overpriced Steam Deck 2.

In the meantime, there’s no shortage of Valve hardware on the market, as the company’s 2026 slate of devices are finally all out in the wild. For more on that, be sure to check out our review of the Steam Frame , as well as why there’s no new Half-Life game .

Bo Moore is IGN's Senior Manager of Tech. You can find him online @usebomswisely.

articles.title: The Steam Frame is $1,059, and Much More Expensive Than It Was Supposed to Be
articles.body:
After nearly a year of waiting, the Steam Frame is finally here. But if you were hoping, despite all the hardware price increases, that the Frame would still sneak under the Valve Index's price, I've got bad news.

The Steam Frame will start at $1,059, which will net you a 256GB headset, powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 processor and 16GB of RAM. If you want more storage, you can get the 1TB model, which will cost $1,299. Either model of the Steam Frame comes with two controllers, an eye spacer for glasses, and a dedicated Wi-Fi 6GHz dongle for PCVR streaming.

Still, that price is likely going to be a dealbreaker for anyone that wanted a Meta Quest 3 killer, but the Frame does have some technology that Meta's headset just doesn't have. The Frame has eye tracking, a dedicated wireless PC dongle, and twice the RAM. The headset is also designed first and foremost for streaming PCVR games, and in my time with the headset, it excels at that. But if you want an affordable VR headset that primarily plays standalone VR games, Meta's headset is probably still the way to go.

Still, among dedicated PCVR headsets, the Steam Frame's price isn't really that outside of the norm. Headsets like the $1,799 Samsung Galaxy XR or the $899 Pimax Crystal Light have a lot of the same capabilities as the Frame, though the latter is wired-only.

Just like with the Steam Machine, it's clear that the Steam Frame is more expensive than Valve was originally planning. When I got a chance to sit down with Valve and talk about the headset , I was told the same thing as when we spoke about the Machine: that the Steam Frame had a similar sort of price increase as Valve's mini PC and handheld . That shouldn't be too surprising, though. With the ongoing RAMpocalypse , prices have only been going up over the last year or so, and even the PS5 and Xbox Series X have been affected.

If you do still want to get your hands on the Steam Frame, it's available for reservation today. Just like with the Steam Machine and Steam Controller , Valve has open reservations, and you can sign up for whichever model you want between now and September 17 at 10am PST . Then, when those initial signups close, Valve will shuffle the entries and split people into a reservation list and a waitlist. If you sign up after the 17th, you'll be added to the back of the waitlist.

The Steam Frame should start shipping out on September 18, and as people on the reservation list get their units, Valve will email folks from the waitlist and move them to the reservation list. If it's anything like the Steam Machine and Steam Controller, though, you can expect the reservation list to be stretched through the end of the year, and probably into the first few months of next year.

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: Valve's Steam Frame Is a Great All-in-One Wireless PCVR Headset, but Is It Worth the Cost?
articles.summary: The Steam Machine is probably one of the first VR headsets that can do everything right out of the box, from standalone gaming to streaming 2D games from your PC. But the high price, short battery life and some software glitches stop it from dethroning the much-cheaper Meta Quest 3.
articles.body:
Valve revealed the Steam Frame, along with the Steam Machine and Controller almost a year ago in November 2025. And while it’s taken quite a long time for all three devices to make it to market, the Frame is finally here to complete the set. Right off the jump, the Steam Frame comes off as just another VR headset, and an excellent one at that, but in the two weeks I’ve spent with this thing, it’s become one of the best ways to play pretty much any game on Steam.

While the Steam Frame’s built-in Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 is strong enough to play a lot of indie games on a 2D virtual screen, where the Frame really shines is when it’s streaming content from a desktop system. Pairing it with a gaming PC strapped with an RTX 5090 and an AMD Ryzen 7 9850X3D , streaming games like The Blood of Dawnwalker or Onimusha to a private theater screen with maxed out settings is probably one of the coolest gaming experiences I’ve had in years.

The problem for a lot of people, though, is going to be the price. When Valve revealed the Steam Frame last year, it said it wanted to keep the price under the $999 Valve Index. But due to a RAM crisis that just doesn’t seem to want to give up, the Frame ultimately came in at $1,059, $60 more than the Index when it came out in 2019.

Just like with seemingly every piece of hardware this year, the Steam Frame’s price is hard to ignore. The headset starts at $1,059, which will net you 256GB of internal storage, or you can get the 1TB model I reviewed here for $1,299. That price is probably going to be a dealbreaker for a lot of people that just want a good standalone VR headset , especially with the $599 Meta Quest 3 on the market.

Then, there’s the $399 PS VR2 , which now technically works with PC, but with lower resolution optics than the Steam Frame (though it is OLED), and a face gasket which has never quite fit me well. Plus, in order to even connect it to your PC, you’re going to need to buy a $79 adapter, and even then you’re going to be hardwired to your PC the entire time you play.

But the Steam Frame is primarily meant to be a wireless PCVR headset with standalone capabilities, rather than the other way around. Valve has put a lot of work into making the wireless PCVR experience as smooth as possible, thanks to the 6GHz wireless dongle included in the box. That, combined with inside-out tracking via the four cameras on the front of the headset, plus internal eye tracking, puts the Steam Frame in competition with dedicated PC headsets like the Samsung Galaxy XR headset or the Play For Dream MR headset, which will set you back $1,799 and $1,999 respectively – albeit with much nicer optics.

I don’t think the Steam Frame is the Meta Quest 3 killer a lot of people were probably hoping it would be, but it is still one of the best headsets I’ve ever used. Whether or not that’s worth the extra cost is ultimately up to you, but after using it for a couple of weeks, I’d buy it in a heartbeat.

I’ve used a lot of VR headsets over the years, and the Steam Frame is easily the most comfortable one I’ve worn. While there are a lot of headsets that feel like they’re pulling your face or weighing down the top of your head, I can wear the Steam Frame for hours without wanting to shove it in a box in the corner.

A lot of that comes down to how light it is. The Steam Frame weighs just 440g, which is 15% lighter than the Meta Quest 3’s 515g. The weight is more evenly distributed, too, thanks to the battery being mounted on the back of the headstrap, rather than on the main unit.

It’s a beautiful headset, with an attractive all-black design and glossy front cover, which holds two of the tracing cameras. Because the battery is located on the strap, the headset doesn’t protrude as far in front of your face as some other wireless headsets.

On the bottom of the headset on either side are two vents, which help keep things cool, and then there’s another, larger vent located up top. When you’re playing standalone games, these vents can get quite warm to the touch, but they do a good job of directing the air away from your face, so you don’t need to worry about getting blasted with hot air.

Behind the vent on the top of the headset, you’ll find an IPD dial. This will let you manually adjust the distance between the lenses in order to make the image clearer and more comfortable to look at. I have a very narrow IPD of around 57mm, and I was surprised that I was able to actually get the headset to adjust to that. There’s even a switch between the two lenses that’ll lock your IPD setting in place, so the lenses don’t move when you’re taking the Frame off or putting it on.

The Steam Frame has pancake lenses with an FoV of up to 110 degrees, which means you have a wide field of vision, which should do a lot to combat motion sickness. As for the display, the Frame has a per-eye resolution of 2160x2160. The refresh rate varies from 72Hz to 120Hz by default, but it can go up to 144Hz via an experimental mode. Most of the time when I was playing a game locally on the Frame, the refresh rate would default to 72Hz, but it would go up to 90Hz or 120Hz when streaming from my PC.

On the right side of the headset (when it's on your face), there are two buttons: a recessed power button, and a button that’ll let you point at things with your face and essentially use the headset itself as a mouse. This sounds like a super niche use case, but it’s actually very useful for when you put your headset on before you turn on the controllers, and need to turn on Room View to see where you put them.

There are two buttons over on the left, too, but those are just volume rockers. I do like that volume is easy to adjust, because the placement of the speakers means sound does tend to leak. The speakers are found right around where the strap meets the headset, and I was immediately worried that they wouldn’t sound great. That worry was unfounded – even when I’m playing games in a loud room, I can still hear everything that’s going on. But, so can anyone else in the room.

Right out of the box, the light seal wasn’t great for me, but Valve also sent me its ergonomic accessories kit, which included a larger light seal. That solved the issue for me immediately, but it does seem like the larger light seal should have just come with the Steam Frame, rather than being part of a $59 accessories pack. Valve said it did this to help keep costs down, but it’s just a little piece of rubber, so I don’t know how much adding a second light seal would have raised the cost.

The face gasket is a pretty standard foam attachment, and while it’s incredibly comfortable I do worry that it’s going to soak up sweat fast , especially if you play a lot of high-movement games like Beat Saber. Luckily, it’s just magnetically attached, and it’s easy to pop off and either wash it or replace with a new one, which Valve will be selling for $59.

The rest of the headset comes apart pretty easily, too. Once you pull off the face gasket, there are three little switches, one at the top and one beneath each lens. Flick those over to the side, and the whole strap assembly slips off of the headset, leaving just the lens and display assembly. I love that the Steam Frame comes apart so easily, because that means it’ll be much easier to clean, or to swap out different elements if something breaks.

Valve also included an expansion bay at the top of the headset, which will allow you to mod the device in ways that I can’t even foresee yet. When I talked to Valve, the Frame’s engineersit told me that there are different camera attachments that are possible, and I’m sure that’s just scratching the surface. There’s also a microSD card reader on the bottom of the headset, so you can expand your internal storage too. Honestly, it really seems like you can do whatever you want with the Steam Frame, and that’s huge.

The strap that comes with the headset does a good job of supporting the weight of the device, and a lot of that has to do with where the battery is mounted. Valve slapped a 21.6Whr battery on the back of the strap, which will sit right on the back of your head while you’re playing. The battery is lined with the same foam as the face gasket, so it’s surprisingly comfortable. I’ve even laid my head back on the battery while playing non-VR games, and if I didn’t already know there was a battery mounted back there, I would never have guessed.

The Steam Frame probably would last a lot longer with a bigger battery, but keeping the battery capacity down makes the headset much lighter, and with how comfortable it is, I can live with charging a little more often. The USB-C port also lives on the battery itself, so even if you want to run a wire to keep it charged, it’ll stay out of your way. Although, I will admit that I basically used the battery life as a reminder to take breaks.

The Steam Frame also comes with new VR controllers, and they look a lot like the Meta Quest 3’s touch controllers. The real difference, though, is that between the two modules, you get a full controller layout. For VR games, that doesn’t matter too much, but if you’re streaming non-VR content from your PC, it means you don’t have to connect a whole new controller just to play games.

There’s plenty of great tech built into the controllers too. They have the same TMR thumbsticks as the Steam Controller, and they feel incredible in games. Valve also worked in some incredible haptics, along with capacitive finger tracking. I’m glad that finger tracking is still there, but you will probably need that accessories kit I mentioned earlier to take full advantage of it. After all, if you loosen your grips on the controllers without the hand straps that come in that kit, you’re just going to drop the controllers.

The controllers also don’t have rechargeable batteries, and are instead powered by a single AA battery each. I actually don’t mind this approach, because it keeps the total amount of cables you need to charge the system down, and you don’t have to worry about the internal battery dying over time, either. It helps that over the course of testing the Steam Frame, the controllers only dropped to 75% battery life, so the batteries will last you a while .

You can always connect a regular controller to the Steam Frame via Bluetooth, but I never felt the urge. There’s just something super chill about kicking back and playing a game on a controller that’s essentially split in half. That’s something that I still love about the Nintendo Switch’s Joy-Cons, and now I can get that experience on PC too.

When Valve first revealed the Steam Frame, I was honestly a little surprised that it was launching a VR headset in 2026. VR gaming has a super dedicated following, to be sure, but it’s not exactly what I’d call a growth category right now. But now that I’ve used the Frame a lot over the last couple weeks, I get what Valve was trying to do here.

One of the problems I’ve always had with VR gaming is that I needed a dedicated device that only really played VR games. That’s always led to headsets collecting dust in my closet after I finish whatever VR game got me to dig it out in the first place. But what makes the Steam Frame different is that it’s great for any type of gaming.

It’s wild that during the process of testing a VR headset, there were entire days I spent with this thing without even touching a VR game. More often than not, I just kicked back and played some Zero Company or Blood of Dawnwalker from my host PC without even thinking about games like Half-Life Alyx .

But at the same time, just by virtue of wearing a VR headset as much as I have been, I’ve been trying out a ton of VR games, like Stellar Cafe, that I otherwise would never have given a second look. In essence, the Steam Frame has become a sort of enhanced gaming monitor, and it’s been a godsend during the last couple weeks, where the hot weather has made me not really want to sit next to my PC and play demanding games. Instead, I can just put on the Frame, sit next to my air conditioner, and play in my own private theater.

Over time, I’m fairly confident this will be the main way I use the Steam Frame, rather than playing VR games. I’ve spent a lot of time with XR glasses like the Viture Beast and the Asus ROG XReal R1 glasses, and the Steam Frame makes them completely irrelevant, at least at home. And, because it can run indie games just as well as a handheld, I can totally see myself taking it on a plane and just playing Hades II – albeit with a battery bank attached.

The Steam Frame is powered by the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3, 16GB of RAM and either 256GB or 1TB of UFS storage. That chip is a bit old at this point, debuting in smartphones all the way back in 2023, but it can still play games. Valve did get SteamOS and Proton running natively on this headset, which is a huge development.

While not every game I tried to run on the headset worked – there were a few, like Darkest Dungeon II , that straight up crashed the entire system – there are plenty you can play natively on the headset without connecting to a PC. Just temper your expectations.

For non-VR games running natively on the Steam Frame, the default setting will limit them to 720p. You can change that, but keep in mind that raising the resolution is just going to be more demanding on the limited GPU. At that default resolution, I’m able to get 120 fps in a game like Hades II, but raising the resolution to 1080p drops that to about 83 fps. And Hades II isn’t exactly what I’d call a demanding game.

There are VR games that will run natively on the headset. I spent a lot of time playing Beat Saber locally on the Steam Frame, and it was awesome. The game felt smooth, and the only time I really felt the urge to stream that game instead was when the battery frequently died after about an hour.

Valve even got Half-Life Alyx running on the Steam Frame, and I’d say it felt good enough . Running Alyx locally on the Frame gives you an image that’s pretty pixelated, and you can tell it's running at a pretty low resolution. And even with lower visual quality, the frame rate is all over the place – sometimes I’d see Alyx hit 80-90 fps, only for it to drop to the 40s in another scene. So while you can play VR games natively, I’d recommend streaming them from your PC instead.

Valve has made a big deal out of its wireless streaming solution for the Steam Frame, and it works wonders. There’s a 6GHz Wi-Fi dongle in the box that will serve as the primary connection to your PC, but the Steam Frame will also connect to your PC via your network. The idea is that, for each packet being sent to and from the Steam Frame, the device will use whichever connection has the lowest latency at that moment.

In practice, it resulted in a rock-solid connection where I couldn’t tell the difference between the Frame standalone and when it was streaming from my PC – at least as far as input lag is concerned. However I did have some growing pains. My PC was initially connected to my network via Wi-Fi, so I’d occasionally get latency spikes. But as soon as I stopped being lazy and connected my PC to my router via ethernet, the problem immediately vanished.

I do wish that the Steam Frame at least had the option to connect to your PC via USB-C instead of only relying on streaming, especially for folks with crowded networks like mine. But at the end of the day it was an issue that was easily solved.

I did end up streaming from my PC way more than playing standalone games, and a lot of that came down to the battery. In the interest of keeping the weight down, the Steam Frame only has a 21.6Whr battery, and it does not last very long at all. Playing Beat Saber locally on the Frame will completely drain the battery after about an hour. There have been a few times where I’d get the little ‘10% remaining’ notification, thinking I could finish the song I was currently playing, only for the screen to go black about a minute later.

When streaming, though, the Steam Frame sips power. I had multiple sessions where I played about two hours of The Blood of Dawnwalker on the virtual screen, and ended the session with about half of my battery remaining. Just another way that makes it feel like the Steam Frame’s standalone mode is just a bonus, rather than the focus.

articles.title: Why There's No New Game for the Steam Frame
articles.body:
When Valve announced the Steam Frame, Machine, and Controller back in November, there was this undercurrent of hope that the company would release some secret new game to complement its new hardware. And, now that the Steam Frame is here, completing this round of Valve hardware, it's clear that there is no new game coming to support it. Instead, Valve is supporting its new VR headset with Half-Life: Alyx, the game that launched with the Valve Index back in 2019.

And with how expensive all of this hardware is , thanks in large part to the ongoing RAM crisis , not having a flagship system-seller makes it hard to imagine that a lot of people are going to rush out to buy it. When I recently sat down with Valve to talk about the Steam Frame , I asked why the headset is launching without a big game to sell it, and was told that the company was focused more on wide compatibility.

That's largely because the Steam Frame is running on a chip that's most often found in smartphones, the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3. Valve software developer Jeff Leinbaugh told me they "really prioritized getting software compatibility in a good state so that there would be a huge number of games, I mean as big as possible, available to play on the device or stream to the device on day one." So, instead of one big launch title, Valve wanted the ARM-based headset to give you "a lot of options of what games to play, whether they're VR games or not VR games."

It's definitely nice that a lot of Steam Games run on ARM, thanks to the dual translation layers of Proton and FEX, but there is a lot of room to grow. There are plenty of 2D games that run well on Valve's headset, but getting system performance ready for standalone VR games is still a work in progress.

To Valve's credit, despite telling us back in November that Half-Life: Alyx would be a lot of work to get running natively on the headset, it did eventually get a 'Steam Frame Verified' certification. Other VR games are more hit or miss, though, and Valve's aware of that.

When I asked Leinbaugh about optimization on the Steam Frame, he told me the work on Alyx is key. "Going through the process of making Alyx run standalone is also helping us figure out the new problem of, 'How do we make sure that VR games running standalone are a good experience?'" Because while getting 2D games like Hades II running natively was a relatively simple optimization process, VR is a bigger struggle.

"For VR, it's kind of a different story because comfort is a bigger factor," Leinbaugh told me. "So as we've gone through the process of making Alyx run better, we're learning about what's important when we look at other VR games to make sure that we can guarantee this is a good experience without setting a bar that's just unreasonably high."

It's clear that Valve is actively working on getting PCVR games that are designed for Windows running on ARM. Just in the two weeks I spent testing the Steam Frame, one of the most popular VR games on the planet, Beat Saber, went from having a big 'unsupported' logo in the UI to having a green checkmark. And now the game runs extremely well, and feels great to play because of how light and balanced the Steam Frame generally is.

So, when Valve says that it was focused on getting compatibility down for the Steam Frame’s launch, it seems like it’s still a work in progress. I’m not sure whether or not having a launch title would have complicated standalone VR optimization further, but it at least sounds like the company is focused on getting that performance down. The Steam Deck certainly had its growing pains when it first came out, and I expect that the Steam Frame will as well.

Luckily, thanks to the 6GHz dongle included in the box, streaming PCVR games from a desktop PC to the Steam Frame is incredible, so that should help paper over the standalone mode’s rough edges for now. And, if all you cared about was standalone VR in the first place, maybe this is your sign to grab a Meta Quest 3 instead.

articles.title: Valve has ported Half-Life: Alyx to ARM, and it’s free with Steam Frame
articles.summary: The Steam Frame headset will come with a native ARM port of Half-Life: Alyx, one of the best VR games that arrived for Windows PCs in 2020.
articles.body: Today, Valve is launching its first headset since 2019 — the new Steam Frame — while dodging our questions about whether it’ll ever make another VR game to go with it. But buyers of the $1,059 gadget will get one flagship VR game anyhow, and it’s great. Every Steam Frame comes with a copy of 2020’s Half-Life: Alyx, one of the best VR games yet made and a good game, period, and you won’t even need a desktop PC — because Valve has ported the entire game to ARM64 so it can run natively on the Frame’s Qualcomm Snapdragon Gen 3 chip. That’s no mean feat: This was a game that required a VR-ready Windows desktop or laptop with a midrange graphics card back in 2020, now running on what’s effectively souped-up smartphone silicon. It even supports all the mods and extra levels that fans have built! My mods and saves were waiting for me the moment I fired it up. The port certainly has compromises in graphical fidelity compared to running it on my desktop, but it manages to feel like a full PC VR game on the Frame in a way that native Meta Quest titles never really have, and without removing any objects or assets. Typically, standalone VR games feel emptier. Valve says (via spokesperson Kaci Aitchison) that’s because the Steam Frame’s built-in eye-tracking cameras unlock foveated rendering — a technique that gives you full resolution where your eyes are actually looking, instead of wasting computing resources on the parts of the image where you’re not: > While we initially didn’t think HL:A running natively on the Steam Frame was likely to be possible, the combination of Foveated Rendering & Eye Tracking turned out to be a silver bullet that enabled us to make it work. The Steam Frame’s 16GB VRAM was also a critical piece, allowing us to avoid having to change any assets, or needing to degrade the gameplay experience. [Image: See how crisp Alyx’s hand is? That’s because that’s where I’m looking. I don’t notice that anything else is low resolution, because as soon as I look, it’s sharp! [Image: [Image: The company says it took “a year of extra software work within the Vulkan drivers and SteamVR” to make it work, but other developers can now take that work and run with it: > The vast majority of that work was not HL:A specific, so it benefits every other game that runs on Steam Frame. Those bug fixes, optimizations, and extra features were all made easier by the open-source nature of the drivers, allowing our team to iterate quickly without having to wait for a third party. [Media: The Steam Frame doesn’t necessarily need games to be ported, though. Like the Steam Deck and Steam Machine, it can play games that were built for Windows through translation and emulation layers that Valve’s been funding for years, and it can run apps originally designed for Android-based headsets through a layer called Lepton as well. Will Valve use this work to build a new VR game of its own? I wouldn’t hold my breath. The Steam Frame is arguably more for flat games than VR ones right now, Valve admitted it was no longer building three full games for VR years ago, and as of 2025, Valve said it had no new VR content in development. Rumor has it that Half-Life 3 has been in very active development, though. Update, September 14th: Digital Foundry has more about the native Alyx port, including that it renders at a base 36fps — though it feels smoother as you turn your head through techniques like reprojection. The headset can refresh at 72Hz or 108Hz for a 2x or 3x multiplier respectively.

articles.title: 'It's Definitely at the Top of Our List' – SteamOS Is Getting Closer to Nvidia Driver Support
articles.body:
One of the biggest goal's of Valve's latest wave of hardware wasn't necessarily to move as many units as possible, but to expand the reach of SteamOS , and it does seem like it's succeeded. There are now two things that are really standing in Valve's way in its quest to dethrone Windows 11 as the de facto gaming OS: anti-cheat and Nvidia graphics drivers. And it looks like the latter is going to be solved soon.

Ahead of Steam Frame's launch, I got a chance to sit down with Valve software developers Pierre-Loup Griffais and Jeff Leinbaugh , and I asked how Nvidia support was coming along.

"Yeah, we're working on it hard," Griffais told me. "It's definitely at the top of our list. It's one of those things just like FEX and working on the Qualcomm driver, it just takes years." That doesn't sound like the driver support is right around the corner, but it does seem like the team has at least got Nvidia GPUs working on the Linux OS, albeit with limited performance.

"We've done a few things like we've enabled the driver now in the main tree of SteamOS," Griffais told me, "so you can get things to light up on certain generations, but in terms of the performance difference between that driver and where the state of the art is, there's definitely still a little bit of a rift that we're trying to work on, but it's getting better day-to-day."

There are certainly versions of Linux that already work with Nvidia drivers, but Team Green's GPUs are always a bit of a hassle on the open-source operating system. Instead, for most people, gaming on Linux works best with AMD graphics cards , as that company has supported drivers on the operating system for years.

But for Valve's goal of getting as many people on SteamOS as possible, getting Nvidia's cards working at full performance is incredibly important. According to the latest Steam Hardware Survey , Nvidia GPUs still make up for 72.88% of Steam's player base. Getting Nvidia graphics cards up and running reliably on SteamOS would be a huge win for Valve.

Hopefully Valve is able to get these graphics cards working as intended on SteamOS soon, and then, maybe, we can finally get anti-cheat support on the operating system. Because, after all, unlocking the operating system for another 72% of the playerbase could cause a huge spike in players migrating from Windows, and that'd be hard to ignore for the Call of Dutys of the world.

articles.title: Valve's Steam Frame is excellent - but at over £1,000 is VR still too expensive?
articles.summary: The BBC's Tom Gerken is hands-on with the latest virtual reality headset.
articles.body:
Valve's new virtual reality headset, the Steam Frame, has officially been released - but it comes at a high price.

The hardware is excellent - a light device which feels comfortable to wear and is packed with clever technology - so long as you're willing to pay a whopping £1,089 for a headset with 1TB of storage.

The variant with 256GB of storage, meanwhile, costs £889.

Both are capable of streaming from a PC as well as playing games on-device, with varying degrees of success.

But it carries a price tag which will make a lot of people roll their eyes, and doesn't do much to dispel criticism that increasingly-costly VR headsets are pricing people out of the hobby.

But before we get into that hefty price tag, is the Steam Frame actually any good?

I've owned VR headsets for well over a decade, and Valve's latest effort makes a promising first impression.

Games run well - really the bare minimum considering the price tag - and it's easy enough to use.

One of the nice things is, like Meta's Quest 3, it has flat "pancake" lenses allowing you to see clearly when you put the headset on.

It's light - weighing little more than a can of soup. But what makes it comfortable is the decision to separate the internals up.

The battery pack rests on the back of your head while the screen is at the front - meaning you don't feel front-heavy, a common criticism of other headsets.

But there are better screens out there. The PlayStation VR2 for example has incredible OLED displays, albeit without the pancake lenses.

Apple and Samsung both have excellent screens too in their own headsets.

Yet these come at a serious premium, costing significantly more than the Steam Frame.

When Meta launched the Quest 3 in June 2023, its 128GB model retailed for £480. Less storage, but a much lower price.

Three years later, it's hard to believe VR just keeps getting more expensive when the Quest 3 felt like a turning point.

"VR today is ultimately a high-end niche," gaming writer Christopher Dring told me.

"Meta had been subsidising the Quest hardware, and it's difficult to imagine they will going forward as they pivot away from those experiences."

Of course, there are reasons for prices going up. AI developers are building giant data centres filled with racks of powerful servers, using many of the same components needed to make devices like the Steam Frame.

Ram prices alone more than doubled in price between October 2025 and the start of 2026 . Meanwhile, the graphics card I bought for £500 a few months ago now sits at closer to £650.

As prices climb higher and higher, hardware developers don't have much of a choice but to put up their own.

"We set out to come out with a device that would have been much more affordable," Valve developer Jeremy Selan said.

"But the global Ram market has impacted us the same way it's impacted everybody."

The Steam Frame is certainly not a budget product.

But not everyone agrees with the suggestion that VR in general costs too much.

"The idea that it's too expensive is one of the biggest misconceptions about VR," UploadVR website editor David Heaney told me.

He pointed out while some headsets may be expensive, Meta's Quest 3S budget model costs £320 but has been on sale for £250 several times.

"In context, a Nintendo Switch 2 is £420, an Xbox Series S is £430, and a PS5 is £470 - Quest 3S, which is primarily used for gaming, is cheaper than other games consoles," he said.

He said the big barrier to more people getting into VR was simply that "we're still in the early days".

"You have to see VR in the same timeframe you'd see personal computers in the 1980s," he said.

"Even if they had been cheap, which they weren't, they weren't yet good enough for mainstream adoption.

"VR is only just getting started, a tech in its 1980s PC era, not something anywhere near maturity."

What makes the Steam Frame really stand out is its new tech, including what developers call its "foveated streaming".

The tech displays only the exact thing you're looking at in the highest quality, while making things in your peripheral vision less clear.

You don't notice the low quality bits because you're not looking at them - saving a massive amount of bandwidth.

It means you can stream VR games wirelessly from your PC in high quality without being tethered by a cable, and it works well.

And it does this while sending two signals at once - combining your household Wi-Fi with a dongle which plugs into your PC.

But then again, you need to spend even more money on a decent PC if you want to benefit from that - which doesn't help with concerns about price.

Valve says despite it being a VR headset, the Steam Frame is not just for VR games.

Selan told me the hope is people will also use it to play their non-VR games too, using the headset as a screen.

I'm not sure I'm convinced developers are going to optimise their non-VR games to run on the headset natively, let alone whether people will sit in their living rooms playing a game on a VR headset rather than their TV.

But it's an interesting thought - and I'd love to be proven wrong.

articles.summary: Bungie's struggles grow more evident as Marathon undergoes more drastic changes, with a move away from seasonal content, a focus on PvE, and a significant delay for the game's next update.
articles.body:
Bungie's struggles grow more evident as Marathon undergoes a handful of drastic changes, with a move away from seasonal content, a focus on PvE, and a significant delay for the game's next update.

Bungie confirmed today that Marathon's next major update, which was slated to release on September 22, will now arrive on December 8. This update will add permanent PvE content, a social space with a firing range, an experimental TDM mode, and much more. On October 6, the game will get a smaller update that resets progression and the in-game economy to prepare for an overhaul.

Bungie noted that it is also moving away from traditional seasonal content updates in order to give the team more time to work on new content. The studio has also been made aware of feedback with regards to keeping players hooked via more depth, variety, and stronger progression, and is actively working to implement changes to respond to that. All in all, it's clear that Bungie is trying its very best to save Marathon amidst major struggles.

Marathon failed to impress players when it launched earlier this year and has only sunk further in the last few months. To make matters worse, Bungie also killed support for its biggest game, Destiny 2, in order to focus more on Marathon . It was a controversial move, and so far, it doesn't seem to be paying off. A swath of players have already written off Marathon, and Bungie's attempt to change the game's identity by moving away from the extraction elements likely won't change minds.

The next big update will be launching just a few weeks after Grand Theft Auto 6 and about two months after the release of Modern Warfare 4, which will have its own expansive extraction component known as DMZ. It's unclear what's in store for the future of Bungie outside of updates to Marathon, as the studio doesn't have anything in full-blown, active production at the moment. Hopes for Destiny 3 were quashed earlier this summer when Bungie laid off a sizable number of developers who were working on Destiny 2 , as well.

articles.title: Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls Director Apologizes for Rough PC Launch and Outlines Upcoming Balance Changes
articles.summary: The director of Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls issued a statement apologizing for the game’s rough launch on PC and outlined upcoming balance adjustments based on the dev team’s findings.
articles.body:
The director of Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls issued a statement apologizing for the game’s rough launch on PC and outlined upcoming balance adjustments based on the dev team’s findings.

Kazuto Sekine, director of Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls, published this statement on Monday, September 14, both in a short post on social media as well as a longer, in-depth blog post on the game’s Steam page .

To start, Sekine apologized for Tokon’s glaring issues on PC when it first released, which were so rough that even massive fighting game streamer Maximilian Dood uninstalled the game during a live broadcast.

Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls Knights of Doom State of Play June 2026 Reveal Trailer - Screenshots

“Seeing the game’s content so positively received, with players enjoying the experience and feeling inspired to keep playing, has been a tremendous source of joy for the entire development team,” Sekine began.

“However, we also recognize that the launch period was impacted by stability issues on PC, and we sincerely apologize for the frustration this has caused our players. It was never our intention for players to be unable to enjoy the game as we envisioned, and we are currently making progress on improvements to the PC version so that everyone can enjoy the game to the fullest.”

He went on to outline a couple of areas the development team believes “need to be addressed,” which included reassessing input responses and concerns of overly-frequent assists and tags.

“We have observed that particular inputs, such as attacks from aerial dashes or Free Flight, would sometimes not register correctly or even at all,” he explained. “To address these issues, we intend to adjust the current input windows to ensure a smoother and more responsive gameplay experience.

“In the current state, there is a 6-frame input buffer when holding a button. However, we intend to adjust the way inputs are handled so that, in certain cases, the action will be performed even when the button is not held.”

When it comes to frequent assists and tags, Sekine admitted that the game was originally balanced with the goal of players constantly tagging their characters in and out of battle. In fact, he revealed that the current state of the game has exceeded their expectations in this regard, though they acknowledged concerns from the community that this might be happening too frequently.

Namely, this means the team is working on increasing the cooldown time for certain assists and switches to “allow us to maintain rushdown capabilities while also creating more time for phases of neutral play.” Sekine said the team is looking into implementing these changes in updates “as soon as possible.”

Changes to overall character balance, however, will be minimal. Sekine and the Tokon team believe that it’s too soon to make sweeping changes, as they are currently in a “discovery phase." Sekine said that it is “still too early to start modifying character traits,” especially since the changes to assists and tags will also impact gameplay.

Read the full message here: Thank you all for your continued passion, patience,… pic.twitter.com/tHw3ymla22 — MARVEL Tōkon: Fighting Souls (@MARVELTokon) September 14, 2026

Tōkon Warriors! Game Director Kazuto “Pachi” Sekine has a message to share with you about our future battle balance update plans for #MARVELTokon : Fighting Souls, and more. Read the full message here: Thank you all for your continued passion, patience,… pic.twitter.com/tHw3ymla22

This is the latest statement from the Tokon team after producer Takeshi Yamanaka apologized for the game’s rough PC launch and admitted that it would be “extremely challenging” to regain players’ trust.

“Unfortunately, in the PC version of the game, there have been in-game issues experienced by many players, which we really apologise to the player base for all of these problems,” he said in an August interview with VGC.

Despite these difficulties, Tokon was well-received critically, with IGN scoring the game a nine out of 10. After Steam reviews stumbled , Arc System Works was quick to push an update that solved many issues for PC players, and has been regularly communicating with the fighting game community in the weeks since then, as evidenced by this latest blog post.

articles.title: I Play Rocky Attempts to Answer the Question of Which Came First, the Rocky or the Sly?
articles.summary: I Play Rocky review: Which came first, the Rocky or the Sly?
articles.body:
This review is based on a screening timed to the Toronto International Film Festival. I Play Rocky will be released in limited theaters on November 6 and expand nationwide on November 20.

Sometimes you can absolutely feel a movie trying oh-so-hard to evoke a reaction out of you and yet still find yourself giving in to that reaction thanks to how skillfully it’s done, and that’s very much the case with I Play Rocky.

This movie’s reason for existence and its intent feels pretty shameless, starting with Amazon MGM wanting to make more use of their Rocky franchise in a somewhat outside-the-box manner (while they wait for Michael B. Jordan to return for another Creed installment ) by putting out their own origin story movie for the original 1976 film. Then there’s the fact that the very unsubtle approach is to hammer home that Sylvester Stallone was writing something deeply personal with Rocky and that hey — if you think about it — Stallone getting the movie made, with him in the starring role no less, was like a real life Rocky story!

Like I said, it’s shameless… But damn it, it sure is effective.

Anthony Ippolito plays Stallone, who we meet in the early 1970s as he’s trying and mostly failing to make it as an actor, frequently being told that he doesn’t have movie star looks, and that his slurred speaking voice especially will stop him from ever being a leading man. His new girlfriend Sasha (AnnaSophia Robb) is the one who suggests that he begin writing screenplays himself, which eventually leads him to write Rocky after he gets a meeting with successful producers Irwin Winkler (P.J. Byrne) and Robert Chartoff (Toby Kebbell), who are encouraged by his previous work.

The first half of I Play Rocky is incredibly engaging as we track the early days of Stallone and Sasha’s relationship, their financial struggles, and his quest to make it as an actor; Stallone hopes his screenplays will help open the door to that future. Ippolito is terrific as Stallone, overcoming the considerable obstacle of playing such a famous and distinct celebrity who has loomed large in pop culture for so long. Yes, he has a strong resemblance to Stallone, and yes, he manages to sound incredibly similar to Stallone; fortunately, this doesn’t feel like just skillful mimicry, but rather a fully formed onscreen character in its own right. Thanks to Ippolito’s grounded performance, you believe in his Sly Stallone’s intelligence, drive, and determination, and you believe in his deep investment in himself, even when it seems like he might be foolishly stubborn.

Robb makes for an excellent onscreen partner for him, bringing a ton of likability and feistiness to Sasha, and completely selling you on both their bond and her own belief in her eventual husband’s talent and potential. Robb gives a wonderfully emotive performance, including an especially well-played scene where she meets Sly’s dad, Frank Sr. (Matt Dillon), for the first time, and we watch as she listens to what’s being said by both men. Robb expertly shows us Sasha painfully realizing just what kind of a verbally and sometimes physically abusive household the man she loves was raised in.

The center of the film focuses heavily on the excitement Winkler and Chartoff have for the Rocky script and the willingness of studio head Sandy Maddox (Tracy Letts as a composite character based on multiple execs) to make it, only to hit a massive impasse thanks to Stallone’s outright refusal to sell the script unless he also gets to star in the movie. There’s some great material here, with Byrne conveying Winkler’s enthusiasm mixed with frustration, and Letts conveying Sandy’s pessimism mixed with intense frustration. The movie gets a lot of comic mileage out of funny moments where these Hollywood veterans are baffled by encountering someone as unwavering as Stallone, who keeps turning down increasingly huge offers.

I Play Rocky is directed by Peter Farrelly from a screenplay by Peter Gamble; it stands out as easily the director’s best film since he and his brother Bobby went their separate ways. Even fans of Farrelly’s Academy Award-winning Green Book (I am not one of them) would likely struggle to love his three straight-to-streaming follow-ups: The Greatest Beer Run Ever, Ricky Stanicky, and Balls Up. I Play Rocky, however, is not only genuinely engaging and heartfelt, but also frequently quite witty, with Farrelly reminding you that he and his brother were once delivering consistently strong comedies like Dumb and Dumber, Kingpin, and There’s Something About Mary.

The second half of I Play Rocky, where we move into the actual production of Rocky, is not quite as strong as the first. We jump through big moments and hurdles in production along the way, such as injuries sustained by Stallone or his trying to film with a non-union crew without being caught (how amusing you find that subplot will likely be fueled by your personal feelings about unions), but it feels a lot more episodic than what came before. There’s also some curious decisions made when it comes to Rocky’s supporting cast, with Carl Weathers (played by an appropriately bombastic Stephan James) given a big entrance via an audition scene followed by multiple looks at the boxing training he went through with Stallone, only to vanish completely from the movie once we’re in the actual scenes on set in which he appeared.

Meanwhile, there’s no depiction at all of the casting of other key Rocky players like Talia Shire (Kiki Seto), Burgess Meredith (Robert Morgan), or Scot Teller (Burt Young), who just appear without introductions or larger context in scenes on the Philadelphia set. This feels particularly odd for Talia, given that Stallone is shown fighting to retain standout moments in the film involving Rocky and Adrian, correctly arguing that they’re pivotal to the movie.

Still, there are some undeniably well done and exciting sequences here as we follow the fast-paced, run-and-gun approach of director John G. Avildsen (Jay Duplass) and the essential work of Garrett Brown (Michael Fuchs), whose still-new steadicam was crucial to pulling off some of the film’s iconic shots such as the run up the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art. In the midst of this, Ippolito is rather remarkable in a sequence where he’s not only asked to replicate one of Stallone’s career-best scenes as an actor but also let us feel the extra meaning behind it to Stallone the man (or at least Stallone the movie character), doing so in a notably impressive and impactful manner.

I Play Rocky ends on a bit of an abrupt note — it feels like it could use an extra scene or two — and you can easily nitpick the way it changes up, streamlines, or alters real-life events and specifics throughout, as you can with any biopic. But even elements that feel like they’re told through rose-colored glasses have a melancholy shadow to them as well, because we know that in real life, Stallone would eventually cheat on Sasha and they’d divorce. We also know that he’d eventually post online tirades against Winkler , calling him untalented and “unhuman” while saying he wanted the rights to Rocky back. But I Play Rocky lets us look back at an earlier time, even if it’s through the haze of nostalgia, and root for both the talented young Sly himself and those around him who helped him oh-so impressively achieve his considerable goals.

Assembly is quick and easy and you should be able to make your first test print in a matter of minutes. No camera is included but, again, there's an official kit to add one .

The multi-filament module fleshes out the 3D printing capabilities and is one of the most important features for any mid to pro level enthusiast. With it you can print using up to four different colored filaments or filament materials simultaneously. It features an intelligent filament system that can identify and manage all four spools seamlessly and independently. Multi-filament add-ons in general cost $200-$300 by themselves, so having an integrated solution will save you a lot of money.
